Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] EvilTokens lure email - inbound message referencing microsoft.com/devicelogin or device code prompts · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Successful Entra ID device code OAuth flow sign-in - EvilTokens authorisation handoff · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Host or user contacting EvilTokens C2 / lure infrastructure (IOC sweep) · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Inbox rule creation immediately following Entra ID device code sign-in · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
EvilTokens lure email - inbound message referencing microsoft.com/devicelogin or device code prompts AIDelivery Medium
Hunts inbound emails carrying EvilTokens phishing lures: messages whose URLs or subject lines reference microsoft.com/devicelogin, 'verify to view' or 'signature required' wording typical of the kit's decoy pages. Article-specific because EvilTokens directs victims to enter the attacker's code at the real Microsoft device login portal. Rationale: Subject wording 'Verify to view' / 'Signature required' and the destination microsoft.com/devicelogin are directly quoted from the article body. Lure-host domains taken from pre-extracted IOC list. Sentinel falls back to OfficeActivity since EmailEvents is a Defender-XDR table not guaranteed in every Sentinel tenant. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.sekoia.io/ • https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity/conditional-access/policy-block-authentication-flows
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1528
Data sourcesEmail
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate IT communications instructing users to activate a new Teams Room or conference-room device via device code
  • Microsoft service notifications referencing devicelogin for setup of Outlook on a new machine
  • DocuSign / Adobe Sign legitimate 'Signature required' notifications
  • Internal phishing-simulation campaigns using the same lure wording
  • Vendor SharePoint share notifications with 'shared document' subject phrasing
Suppression filter
| where SenderFromDomain !in~ ("microsoft.com","docusign.net","adobesign.com") and SenderFromAddress !endswith "@yourorg.com"
Response runbook
Triage: pull the full message via EmailEvents.NetworkMessageId, compare SenderFromAddress vs SenderMailFromAddress for spoofing, review SPF/DKIM/DMARC, and check UrlClickEvents for whether any recipient actually clicked. Contain: ZAP-purge the message for all recipients, block the sender domain at the gateway, and tenant-block the lure URL. If any recipient clicked, immediately revoke their Entra sessions, invalidate refresh tokens, and reset MFA. Hunt: pivot on RecipientEmailAddress into SigninLogs over the next 24h looking for successful deviceCode authentications; if found, escalate to the EvilTokens account-takeover playbook and audit for new inbox rules + OAuth app consents.
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound" and DeliveryAction in ("Delivered","DeliveredAsSpam")
| where Subject has_any ("verify to view","signature required","device code","devicelogin","shared document","signature requested")
| join kind=inner (
    EmailUrlInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where Url has_any ("microsoft.com/devicelogin","oauth2/deviceauth","authdocspro.com","backdoor-hub.com","docusend.networkssolutionmail.com","eventcalender-schedule.com","evobothub.org","framebound.cloud","infinitechai.org","notificationsmanagersec.com","internalmemorecord.bxwancheng.com","newmobilepolojean.com")
) on NetworkMessageId
| project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromAddress, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, Url, UrlDomain, DeliveryAction, AuthenticationDetails
| order by Timestamp desc
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
| where Operation in ("Send","MailItemsAccessed","Create")
| where Subject has_any ("verify to view","signature required","device code","devicelogin","shared document")
   or Parameters has_any ("microsoft.com/devicelogin","authdocspro.com","notificationsmanagersec.com","eventcalender-schedule.com","evobothub.org","framebound.cloud","infinitechai.org","backdoor-hub.com","docusend.networkssolutionmail.com")
| project TimeGenerated, Operation, Sender, P2Sender, Recipients, Subject, UserId, ClientIP, UserAgent, Parameters
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Successful Entra ID device code OAuth flow sign-in - EvilTokens authorisation handoff AIExploitation High
Detects successful Entra ID sign-ins that completed via the OAuth 2.0 device authorization grant. EvilTokens abuses this exact flow: the attacker requests a device code, the victim authenticates it on microsoft.com/devicelogin, and Microsoft issues access + refresh tokens to the attacker's session. Device code auth is rare in normal corporate use, making any success a high-fidelity hunt pivot. Rationale: Article states EvilTokens 'abuses the OAuth 2.0 device authorization grant flow' and that 'Microsoft issues access and refresh tokens to the session opened by the attacker'. Successful deviceCode auth is rare in normal enterprise use, so a clean match is high-fidelity. Cross-checked with Sekoia and Microsoft device-code-flow Conditional Access guidance. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.sekoia.io/ • https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity/conditional-access/policy-block-authentication-flows • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1528/
ATT&CKT1528 T1078.004 T1566
Data sourcesAuthentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Teams Room / Surface Hub / conference-room device enrollment using device code flow
  • Help-desk-assisted sign-in to an Azure VM via Azure CLI device code
  • Developer / sysadmin using 'az login --use-device-code' on a remote host
  • First-time setup of legitimate IoT devices (digital signage, printers) against the tenant
  • PowerShell automation using Microsoft Graph SDK device code authentication during migrations
Suppression filter
| where AppDisplayName !in~ ("Microsoft Teams Rooms","Surface Hub","Azure CLI") and DeviceDetail !has "Teams Room"
Response runbook
Triage: pull the SigninLogs entry for the request, check IPAddress geolocation and ASN against the user's normal pattern, identify the AppDisplayName (Microsoft Graph / Azure CLI / Office Apps are most-abused), and search for the preceding EvilTokens lure email to the same UPN. Contain: immediately revoke the user's sessions via Revoke-AzureADUserAllRefreshToken, invalidate refresh tokens via Graph API, force password reset and MFA re-registration. Hunt: search OfficeActivity for inbox-rule creation, mailbox-forwarding setup, and mass-download events within 24h of the sign-in; review OAuth consent grants for the affected UPN; pivot on the source IP across all tenant sign-ins for additional victims.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ErrorCode == 0
| extend AuthDetailsStr = tostring(AuthenticationDetails)
| extend AuthProcessingStr = tostring(AuthenticationProcessingDetails)
| where AuthDetailsStr has "deviceCode" or AuthProcessingStr has "deviceCode" or AuthenticationRequirement has "deviceCode"
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, Country, City, Application, AppDisplayName, ApplicationId, UserAgent, DeviceName, AadDeviceId, IsAnonymousProxy, RiskLevelDuringSignIn, RiskState, ConditionalAccessStatus, AuthDetailsStr
| order by Timestamp desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == 0
| extend AuthDetailsStr = tostring(AuthenticationDetails)
| extend AuthProcessingStr = tostring(AuthenticationProcessingDetails)
| where AuthDetailsStr has "deviceCode" or AuthProcessingStr has "deviceCode" or AuthenticationRequirement has "deviceCode"
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, UserDisplayName, IPAddress, Location, AppDisplayName, AppId, ResourceDisplayName, ClientAppUsed, UserAgent, DeviceDetail, AutonomousSystemNumber, RiskLevelDuringSignIn, RiskState, ConditionalAccessStatus, OriginalRequestId, AuthDetailsStr
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Host or user contacting EvilTokens C2 / lure infrastructure (IOC sweep) AICommand & Control Medium
Sweeps network/DNS telemetry for outbound contact to EvilTokens phishing/C2 IPs and domains from the article's IOC list. Article-specific because these are exactly the indicators tied to the kit's active campaigns since February 2026, including the March 2026 campaign hitting 340+ organisations. Rationale: All IPs and domains are taken verbatim from the article's pre-extracted IOC list, tied to EvilTokens campaigns documented by Sekoia and Microsoft Threat Intel. Sweep covers both initial lure-page contact and any post-tokenization C2/redirector traffic. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.sekoia.io/ • https://threatfox.abuse.ch/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1566.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate marketing / SaaS traffic if any listed domain is later reclaimed by a benign owner
  • Security researchers / sandbox detonation environments inside the org browsing IOC URLs intentionally
  • Proxy/inspection-bypass services briefly resolving the domains as part of TI feed enrichment
  • Email security gateways pre-rendering URLs in inbound mail (URL detonation rather than user click)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","SenseIR.exe","smartscreen.exe")
Response runbook
Triage: identify the initiating process and user (InitiatingProcessAccountUpn / ContextImageFileName) — browser is expected for lure-page hits, anything else is more concerning. Cross-reference with EmailEvents to find the originating message and with SigninLogs for any device code success in the next 60 minutes. Contain: block the indicators at the proxy/firewall/DNS layer, isolate the host if a non-browser process generated the hit, and force session revocation + token invalidation for the involved user. Hunt: expand IOC pivot by 30 days, look for newly registered look-alike domains on the same name servers, query OAuth consent grants and inbox rules for the user, and submit the indicators to internal TI for cross-tenant sweep.

(CommonSecurityLog

Inbox rule creation immediately following Entra ID device code sign-in AIActions on Objectives High
Correlates a successful Entra ID deviceCode sign-in with the creation of a new mailbox inbox rule for the same user within 60 minutes. EvilTokens operators routinely set hide/forward/delete rules post-tokenization to stage BEC against finance, HR, logistics and sales mailboxes — this combination is the article's specific post-compromise tell. Rationale: Article explicitly warns to 'watch for unusual device-code authentication ... and new inbox rules' and ties post-tokenization actions to BEC preparation against finance/HR/logistics/sales mailboxes. The 60-minute join window encodes that the inbox rule is part of the same takeover session. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.sekoia.io/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1564/008/
ATT&CKT1564.008 T1114.003 T1528
Data sourcesAuthentication Change
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User self-service Outlook rules created shortly after a legitimate Surface Hub / Teams Room device code authentication
  • Migration scripts using device code auth to programmatically configure inbox rules for users
  • Sysadmin re-provisioning an account via Microsoft Graph SDK device code login
  • Anti-spam / mailbox-cleanup vendor tooling that authenticates via device code and configures rules
  • Legitimate executive assistant configuring rules on a delegated mailbox right after sign-in
Suppression filter
| where Parameters !has "Stop-Processing" and AppDisplayName !in~ ("Outlook Web App","Microsoft Office")
Response runbook
Triage: pull the full inbox rule JSON from Parameters/RawEventData — hide/forward/delete rules with single-character names or names like '. ' / '!' are textbook EvilTokens BEC staging. Identify the source IP and ASN of the device code sign-in. Contain: revoke all sessions and refresh tokens for the user (Revoke-AzureADUserAllRefreshToken + Disconnect-MgGraph), disable the malicious inbox rule via Remove-InboxRule, and reset the account password and MFA registration. Hunt: search the user's mailbox for sent items in the rule window for outbound BEC attempts, audit other Entra users for the same source IP, and run a 30-day OfficeActivity sweep for matching rule patterns across the tenant.
let DeviceCodeSignIns = AADSignInEventsBeta
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where ErrorCode == 0
    | extend AuthDetailsStr = tostring(AuthenticationDetails)
    | where AuthDetailsStr has "deviceCode" or AuthenticationRequirement has "deviceCode"
    | project DeviceCodeTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Application;
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("New-InboxRule","Set-InboxRule","UpdateInboxRules")
| extend RuleDetails = tostring(RawEventData)
| where RuleDetails has_any ("DeleteMessage","MoveToFolder","ForwardTo","RedirectTo","MarkAsRead")
   or RuleDetails has_any ("RSS Feeds","Archive","Conversation History",".. ","!")
| join kind=inner DeviceCodeSignIns on $left.AccountDisplayName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (DeviceCodeTime .. DeviceCodeTime + 60m)
| extend DelayMinutes = datetime_diff('minute', Timestamp, DeviceCodeTime)
| project DeviceCodeTime, RuleCreatedTime = Timestamp, DelayMinutes, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, Application, ActionType, ObjectName, RuleDetails
| order by RuleCreatedTime desc
let DeviceCodeSignIns = SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where ResultType == 0
    | extend AuthDetailsStr = tostring(AuthenticationDetails)
    | where AuthDetailsStr has "deviceCode" or AuthenticationRequirement has "deviceCode"
    | project DeviceCodeTime = TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName = tolower(UserPrincipalName), IPAddress, AppDisplayName, OriginalRequestId;
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Operation in ("New-InboxRule","Set-InboxRule","UpdateInboxRules")
| extend UserPrincipalName = tolower(UserId)
| where Parameters has_any ("DeleteMessage","MoveToFolder","ForwardTo","RedirectTo","MarkAsRead")
| join kind=inner DeviceCodeSignIns on UserPrincipalName
| where TimeGenerated between (DeviceCodeTime .. DeviceCodeTime + 60m)
| extend DelayMinutes = datetime_diff('minute', TimeGenerated, DeviceCodeTime)
| project DeviceCodeTime, RuleCreatedTime = TimeGenerated, DelayMinutes, UserPrincipalName, ClientIP, IPAddress, AppDisplayName, Operation, Parameters
| order by RuleCreatedTime desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web

     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

         by Processes.dest, Processes.user

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email

    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |

    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`

Sniper Dz Scams Target MENA Users via Fake Facebook Offers and Browser Alerts

The Hacker News
2026-06-15 8 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of fraudulent activity targeting users across the Middle East and North Africa by employing various fraudulent Facebook accounts impersonating politicians, public figures, and trusted organizations. "These accounts promoted fake offers, including free mobile internet packages, financial compensation, and government subsidy programs," Group-IB

IPs65.60.9.236 108.178.23.118 184.154.10.254

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Sniper Dz PhaaS infrastructure delivered via inbound email URLs · [LLM] User click-through on Sniper Dz redirect URL (Safe Links) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] DNS or network egress to Sniper Dz infrastructure (IP and host indicators) · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Sniper Dz PhaaS infrastructure delivered via inbound email URLs AIDelivery High
Inbound message contains a URL pointing to known Sniper Dz redirector or landing-page infrastructure (sniperdz.com, raviral.com, win.feezossl.xyz, etc.). Hunts the delivery vector even when the lure was originally posted on Facebook and forwarded to the victim via mail share. Group-IB tied these domains to the post-INTERPOL-takedown resurgence of the kit. Rationale: Uses the specific IOC domains the article enumerates as Sniper Dz infrastructure. Inbound + URL-domain match on a curated list is high-fidelity because these are not generic services; the only FP risk is a security analyst forwarding the IOC list internally.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1583.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security analyst forwarding the IOC list or Group-IB write-up via email
  • Threat-intel digest emails that quote the URLs verbatim (Recorded Future, Group-IB newsletter)
  • Phishing-simulation vendor URLs that intentionally mimic these domains for awareness training
  • User reporting the phishing email back through a Report Phish add-in (causes the same URL to traverse the wire again)
Suppression filter
| where SenderFromAddress !endswith "@yourorg.com" and RecipientEmailAddress !in~ ("soc@yourorg.com","phishing-reports@yourorg.com","abuse@yourorg.com")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): pull the full recipient list for the matching NetworkMessageId via EmailEvents and check whether any of them subsequently appear in UrlClickEvents for the same NetworkMessageId — that escalates this from delivery to click-through. Step 2 (contain): soft-delete or quarantine outstanding copies via Defender Threat Explorer for the NetworkMessageId, and add the matched UrlDomain values to the tenant block list. Step 3 (hunt): pivot to DeviceNetworkEvents/DnsEvents on the same domains for the last 14 days across the recipient population to find anyone who opened the URL outside Safe Links (clicked from mobile, copy-pasted into another browser).
let SniperDzDomains = dynamic(["sniperdz.com","raviral.com","offer.raviral.com","win.feezossl.xyz","win.anababayala.com","aff.bnaosf1he.shop","automaticgiveaway.000webhostapp.com","facebookbusiness0078.blogspot.be","dev-cdn370.pantheonsite.io"]);
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| join kind=inner (
    EmailUrlInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | extend HostLower = tolower(UrlDomain)
    | where HostLower has_any (SniperDzDomains) or Url has_any (SniperDzDomains)
    | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain, ReportId
  ) on NetworkMessageId
| project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromAddress, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation, Url, UrlDomain
| order by Timestamp desc
let SniperDzDomains = dynamic(["sniperdz.com","raviral.com","offer.raviral.com","win.feezossl.xyz","win.anababayala.com","aff.bnaosf1he.shop","automaticgiveaway.000webhostapp.com","facebookbusiness0078.blogspot.be","dev-cdn370.pantheonsite.io"]);
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DeviceVendor in~ ("Proofpoint","Mimecast","Cisco","Microsoft")
| where RequestURL has_any (SniperDzDomains) or DestinationHostName has_any (SniperDzDomains) or Message has_any (SniperDzDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceUserName, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, DestinationHostName, Activity, DeviceAction, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Sniper Dz PhaaS URL in Inbound Mail
id: 9c64b0e0-2a3a-4a3a-9c64-b0e02a3a4a3a
status: experimental
description: Detects inbound email carrying a URL belonging to Sniper Dz phishing-as-a-service infrastructure (post-INTERPOL takedown resurgence reported by Group-IB June 2026).
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/sniper-dz-scams-target-mena-users-via.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/15
tags:
  - attack.initial_access
  - attack.t1566.002
logsource:
  category: email
  product: m365
detection:
  selection:
    EmailDirection: 'Inbound'
  url_match:
    Url|contains:
      - 'sniperdz.com'
      - 'raviral.com'
      - 'win.feezossl.xyz'
      - 'win.anababayala.com'
      - 'aff.bnaosf1he.shop'
      - 'automaticgiveaway.000webhostapp.com'
      - 'facebookbusiness0078.blogspot.be'
      - 'dev-cdn370.pantheonsite.io'
  condition: selection and url_match
level: high
source:(email OR office365.email OR proofpoint OR mimecast) (@url:(*sniperdz.com* OR *raviral.com* OR *win.feezossl.xyz* OR *win.anababayala.com* OR *aff.bnaosf1he.shop* OR *automaticgiveaway.000webhostapp.com* OR *facebookbusiness0078.blogspot.be* OR *dev-cdn370.pantheonsite.io*) OR @message.url:(*sniperdz.com* OR *raviral.com* OR *win.feezossl.xyz* OR *win.anababayala.com* OR *aff.bnaosf1he.shop*))
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(All_Email.url) as url values(All_Email.subject) as subject values(All_Email.src_user) as src_user from datamodel=Email.All_Email where All_Email.url IN ("*sniperdz.com*","*raviral.com*","*win.feezossl.xyz*","*win.anababayala.com*","*aff.bnaosf1he.shop*","*automaticgiveaway.000webhostapp.com*","*facebookbusiness0078.blogspot.be*","*dev-cdn370.pantheonsite.io*") by All_Email.recipient All_Email.message_id | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(All_Email.url) as url values(All_Email.subject) as subject values(All_Email.src_user) as src_user from datamodel=Email.All_Email where All_Email.url IN ("*sniperdz.com*","*raviral.com*","*win.feezossl.xyz*","*win.anababayala.com*","*aff.bnaosf1he.shop*","*automaticgiveaway.000webhostapp.com*","*facebookbusiness0078.blogspot.be*","*dev-cdn370.pantheonsite.io*") by All_Email.recipient All_Email.message_id | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
User click-through on Sniper Dz redirect URL (Safe Links) AIDelivery High
Safe Links UrlClickEvents for one of the Sniper Dz infrastructure domains, including ClickedThrough where the user bypassed the warning. This is the highest-fidelity post-delivery signal in the kill chain and the one that warrants immediate user contact, because the next step in the article's described funnel is browser-notification permission grant and TDS routing. Rationale: UrlClickEvents is the only Defender table that confirms the user actually opened the link (vs. it merely landed in their inbox). IsClickedThrough==true is an extra escalation signal because Safe Links warned them and they proceeded anyway — high-priority user-contact case. Domains are taken verbatim from the article's IOC list. Sentinel has no equivalent table without M365 Defender, so sentinel_kql is intentionally empty.
ATT&CKT1204.001
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security analyst manually clicking the URL inside Safe Links during triage of UC1
  • Phishing-reporter user clicking the link before reporting (legitimate but operationally noisy)
  • Web-content categorisation services that crawl through Safe Links
  • Sandbox / detonation vendor accounts that follow URLs from quarantined mail
Suppression filter
| where AccountUpn !in~ ("soc-analyst@yourorg.com","ir-handler@yourorg.com") and IPAddress !in ("<known-sandbox-egress-ips>")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): identify AccountUpn and pull DeviceInfo to map to device; pull DeviceNetworkEvents on the user's primary device for the 30 min after ClickTime — look for follow-on traffic to the redirect chain or notification-service VAPID endpoints. Step 2 (contain): reset the user's session cookies for the mail tenant and force MFA re-prompt; if the user reports they granted browser-notification permission, push a managed-browser policy that revokes notification grants for the IOC domains. Step 3 (hunt): pivot on the matched Url back to EmailEvents/EmailUrlInfo on the same NetworkMessageId to identify the original sender and other recipients; check for secondary clicks from the same campaign within 24h across the tenant.
let SniperDzDomains = dynamic(["sniperdz.com","raviral.com","offer.raviral.com","win.feezossl.xyz","win.anababayala.com","aff.bnaosf1he.shop","automaticgiveaway.000webhostapp.com","facebookbusiness0078.blogspot.be","dev-cdn370.pantheonsite.io"]);
UrlClickEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
| extend UrlLower = tolower(Url)
| where UrlLower has_any (SniperDzDomains)
| join kind=leftouter (
    EmailEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | project NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, Subject, RecipientEmailAddress
  ) on NetworkMessageId
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, ActionType, IsClickedThrough, Workload, SenderFromAddress, Subject
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
let SniperDzDomains = dynamic(["sniperdz.com","raviral.com","offer.raviral.com","win.feezossl.xyz","win.anababayala.com","aff.bnaosf1he.shop","automaticgiveaway.000webhostapp.com","facebookbusiness0078.blogspot.be","dev-cdn370.pantheonsite.io"]);
UrlClickEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
| extend UrlLower = tolower(Url)
| where UrlLower has_any (SniperDzDomains)
| join kind=leftouter (
    EmailEvents
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | project NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, Subject, RecipientEmailAddress
  ) on NetworkMessageId
| project TimeGenerated, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, ActionType, IsClickedThrough, Workload, SenderFromAddress, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
DNS or network egress to Sniper Dz infrastructure (IP and host indicators) AICommand & Control Medium
Direct EDR/DNS observation of a workstation contacting one of the Sniper Dz hosting IPs (65.60.9.236, 108.178.23.118, 184.154.10.254) or attempting to resolve one of the named scam domains. Catches the case where the user reached the link outside Safe Links (mobile mail, SMS lure, Facebook in-app browser) and only the network egress survives. Rationale: Article enumerates three IPs (65.60.9.236, 108.178.23.118, 184.154.10.254) and nine domains as the campaign's hosting / redirect / TDS infrastructure. IP-membership + DNS-query-name match is the cleanest IOC pivot available and survives the scenario where Safe Links never observed the click (mobile, SMS lure, Facebook in-app browser).
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1583.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel feed ingestion box pulling the same IOCs from an OSINT source (e.g. abuse.ch fetch)
  • Researcher sandbox detonating the URLs from a corporate egress
  • URL-scanning service (urlscan, VirusTotal) called from an internal pipeline that resolves IOC domains
  • Pantheonsite.io is shared-tenant hosting — false positives possible if dev-cdn370.pantheonsite.io is later reassigned to a legitimate customer (revalidate domain ownership quarterly)
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in ("<threat-intel-sandbox-hostnames>") and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("curl.exe","wget.exe","powershell.exe") | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("svc-threatintel","svc-urlscan")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): identify the device, the user, and the originating process — if InitiatingProcessFileName is a browser (msedge.exe/chrome.exe/firefox.exe) check UrlClickEvents and EmailEvents for the same user within the prior 30 min to identify the lure source; if it's a non-browser process, treat as elevated severity. Step 2 (contain): block the IPs at perimeter and the domains in the secure web gateway / DNS resolver; revoke browser notification permission via managed policy for affected users. Step 3 (hunt): pivot on the user across DeviceNetworkEvents/DnsEvents for related redirect domains (Linktree / Linkbio destinations that ended in the same IPs), and across the wider population for any device that resolved any of the IOC domains in the last 30 days.
let SniperDzIPs = dynamic(["65.60.9.236","108.178.23.118","184.154.10.254"]);
let SniperDzDomains = dynamic(["sniperdz.com","raviral.com","offer.raviral.com","win.feezossl.xyz","win.anababayala.com","aff.bnaosf1he.shop","automaticgiveaway.000webhostapp.com","facebookbusiness0078.blogspot.be","dev-cdn370.pantheonsite.io"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in (SniperDzIPs)
   or (isnotempty(RemoteUrl) and tolower(RemoteUrl) has_any (SniperDzDomains))
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
let SniperDzIPs = dynamic(["65.60.9.236","108.178.23.118","184.154.10.254"]);
let SniperDzDomains = dynamic(["sniperdz.com","raviral.com","offer.raviral.com","win.feezossl.xyz","win.anababayala.com","aff.bnaosf1he.shop","automaticgiveaway.000webhostapp.com","facebookbusiness0078.blogspot.be","dev-cdn370.pantheonsite.io"]);
union isfuzzy=true
( DnsEvents
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where tolower(Name) has_any (SniperDzDomains)
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Indicator=Name, Source="DnsEvents" ),
( ImDnsActivity
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where tolower(DnsQuery) has_any (SniperDzDomains)
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer=SrcHostname, ClientIP=SrcIpAddr, Indicator=DnsQuery, Source="ImDnsActivity" ),
( CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where DestinationIP in (SniperDzIPs) or tolower(DestinationHostName) has_any (SniperDzDomains) or tolower(RequestURL) has_any (SniperDzDomains)
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer=SourceHostName, ClientIP=SourceIP, Indicator=coalesce(DestinationHostName, RequestURL, DestinationIP), Source="CommonSecurityLog" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: DNS Resolution to Sniper Dz PhaaS Domain
id: 1f5a7c44-9a7e-4cba-bc88-7f9c6a3b2e44
status: experimental
description: Detects DNS queries to known Sniper Dz scam infrastructure reported by Group-IB (June 2026), targeting MENA users via fake Facebook offers.
references:

author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/15
tags:

  - attack.t1071.001

source:(windows.sysmon OR linux.auditd OR zeek OR suricata OR netflow) (@DestinationIp:(65.60.9.236 OR 108.178.23.118 OR 184.154.10.254) OR @DestinationHostname:(*sniperdz.com OR *raviral.com OR *win.feezossl.xyz OR *win.anababayala.com OR *aff.bnaosf1he.shop OR *automaticgiveaway.000webhostapp.com OR *facebookbusiness0078.blogspot.be OR *dev-cdn370.pantheonsite.io) OR @dns.question.name:(*sniperdz.com OR *raviral.com OR *win.feezossl.xyz OR *win.anababayala.com OR *aff.bnaosf1he.shop OR *automaticgiveaway.000webhostapp.com OR *facebookbusiness0078.blogspot.be OR *dev-cdn370.pantheonsite.io))

NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(All_Traffic.dest) as dest values(All_Traffic.dest_ip) as dest_ip values(All_Traffic.src) as src values(All_Traffic.user) as user values(All_Traffic.app) as app from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where (All_Traffic.dest_ip IN ("65.60.9.236","108.178.23.118","184.154.10.254") OR All_Traffic.dest IN ("sniperdz.com","raviral.com","offer.raviral.com","win.feezossl.xyz","win.anababayala.com","aff.bnaosf1he.shop","automaticgiveaway.000webhostapp.com","facebookbusiness0078.blogspot.be","dev-cdn370.pantheonsite.io")) by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.user | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(All_Traffic.dest) as dest values(All_Traffic.dest_ip) as dest_ip values(All_Traffic.src) as src values(All_Traffic.user) as user values(All_Traffic.app) as app from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where (All_Traffic.dest_ip IN ("65.60.9.236","108.178.23.118","184.154.10.254") OR All_Traffic.dest IN ("sniperdz.com","raviral.com","offer.raviral.com","win.feezossl.xyz","win.anababayala.com","aff.bnaosf1he.shop","automaticgiveaway.000webhostapp.com","facebookbusiness0078.blogspot.be","dev-cdn370.pantheonsite.io")) by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.user | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
CVE-2026-0257 GlobalProtect PoC Client-Config Signature (Win10 Pro 64-bit + empty domain) AIExploitation High
Hunts the article's primary detection guidance: successful GlobalProtect gateway-connected events whose client posture carries the hard-coded PoC values endpoint_os_version='Microsoft Windows 10 Pro 64-bit' AND empty source_user_info.domain. Real users almost never connect with both an empty domain and that exact Win10 Pro string simultaneously. Rationale: Uses the two PoC client-config strings Palo Alto Networks explicitly told customers to search for in GlobalProtect logs (endpoint_os_version='Microsoft Windows 10 Pro 64-bit' + empty source_user_info.domain). Both conditions together are essentially unique to the PoC. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/palo-alto-warns-of-active-exploitation.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication Network_Sessions.All_Sessions
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal pentest replay of the public PoC against a corporate GP gateway during an authorized assessment
  • Engineering test rigs imaged with a generic Win10 Pro template and joined to no AD domain (workgroup laptops)
  • Lab/QA GlobalProtect clients used by network engineers validating gateway upgrades with default client builds
  • Legitimate BYOD / contractor laptop running Windows 10 Pro never joined to a domain
Suppression filter
| where SourceUserName !in~ ('pentest-svc', 'redteam-lab', 'gp-test') | where SourceIP !in ('10.0.0.0/8', '192.168.0.0/16')
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the SourceIP and SourceUserName from the hit and confirm whether the account is real, whether it normally connects from a domain-joined endpoint, and whether the source IP appears in the article's IOC list. 2) Contain: revoke active GlobalProtect sessions for the user, force a password+MFA reset, and block the source IP at the perimeter firewall pending investigation. Verify the appliance is patched against CVE-2026-0257. 3) Hunt: pivot on the source IP across firewall, IIS, and AAD logs for the past 60 days; look for additional gateway-connected events from the same IP under other usernames (credential spray pattern), and search internal traffic from the VPN-assigned IP for reconnaissance behaviour even though Palo Alto Networks reports no post-access activity yet.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where DeviceVendor has 'Palo Alto'
| where DeviceProduct has 'GlobalProtect' or Message has 'GlobalProtect'
| where Message has 'gateway-connected'
| where Message has 'Microsoft Windows 10 Pro 64-bit'
| where Message has 'source_user_info.domain='
| where Message has_any ('source_user_info.domain=;', 'source_user_info.domain= ', 'source_user_info.domain=,', 'source_user_info.domain=|', 'source_user_info.domain=empty')
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DeviceAction, Activity, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

GlobalProtect Gateway/Portal Traffic From CVE-2026-0257 Attack Infrastructure IPs AIDelivery Medium
Watches firewall + endpoint telemetry for any traffic involving the nine IP addresses Palo Alto Networks attributed to active CVE-2026-0257 exploitation. Hits represent either inbound exploitation attempts against your GP portal or outbound traffic from an internal host to the same infrastructure. Rationale: Direct hard match against the nine IOC IPs Palo Alto Networks published as confirmed CVE-2026-0257 attack infrastructure. Inbound hits = exploitation attempt; outbound from internal hosts = potential beacon to attacker infra. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/palo-alto-warns-of-active-exploitation.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • VPN-related troubleshooting / TAC support sessions where an engineer connects out to one of the IPs to validate the IOC list
  • Researcher / threat-hunter VM in your network actively probing the listed IPs for IOC enrichment
  • Stale NAT or shared-hosting reuse — one of the IPs is later assigned to a benign cloud customer your users legitimately reach
  • Honeypot or sandbox infrastructure your team operates that happens to share an IP range
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ('threathunter.exe', 'curl.exe', 'powershell_ise.exe') | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ('threat-research', 'soc-analyst')
Response runbook
1) Triage: determine direction — inbound to the GP portal or outbound from an internal endpoint. For inbound, confirm whether any of the same IPs produced a successful gateway-connected event in the last 30 days. For outbound, identify the source host and process. 2) Contain: block all nine IPs at the perimeter firewall and at any cloud egress gateway; if outbound, isolate the source endpoint immediately and preserve memory. 3) Hunt: search 60 days of firewall + proxy + DNS for any historical contact with these IPs; pull GlobalProtect logs for all successful gateway-connected events from these IPs and correlate to the PoC-signature detection above; check whether any of the source IPs probed other public services in your perimeter.

GlobalProtect Session With CVE-2026-0257 PoC Default Hostnames (WINDOWS-LAPTOP-001 / DESKTOP-GP01 / GP-CLIENT) AIExploitation High
Detects gateway-connected GlobalProtect events whose reported client hostname matches the three textbook PoC defaults disclosed by Palo Alto Networks. No real enterprise asset inventory contains these exact names. Rationale: These three hostnames are PoC scaffolding values explicitly named in the article's IOC list — they are functionally indistinguishable from canaries. A real client almost never reports these as its NetBIOS/host_id. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/palo-alto-warns-of-active-exploitation.html
ATT&CKT1133 T1190
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Newly imaged corporate laptop that hasn't received its asset-tag rename yet (rare; investigate anyway)
  • QA / staging GlobalProtect test client a network engineer named generically
  • Cloud-based VDI golden image whose hostname template literally happens to be DESKTOP-GP01
  • Asset built from an off-the-shelf Win10 install with the installer-generated default DESKTOP-XXXXXXX placeholder
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the SourceIP and SourceUserName for each hit. Look up the username in IAM/HR — is the account active, and does the user own a real corporate laptop? Check whether the public_ip overlaps with the nine known attacker IPs. 2) Contain: kill the GP session, disable the account pending investigation, and block the source public IP. 3) Hunt: search 90 days for any prior gateway-connected event using the same hostname against any account; pivot on the SourceIP to find other compromised accounts; cross-check with the PoC-signature detection (Win10 Pro 64-bit + empty domain).
DeviceInfo
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where DeviceName in~ ('WINDOWS-LAPTOP-001', 'DESKTOP-GP01', 'GP-CLIENT')
| project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, OSPlatform, OSVersion, PublicIP, LoggedOnUsers, IsAzureADJoined
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DeviceVendor has 'Palo Alto'
| where Message has_any ('WINDOWS-LAPTOP-001', 'DESKTOP-GP01', 'GP-CLIENT')
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DeviceAction, Activity, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

GlobalProtect Session Reporting Vendor-Default Placeholder MAC Address AIExploitation High
Hunts GlobalProtect HIP / host-info logs for the two textbook placeholder MAC addresses listed in the IOC bundle (aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff and 00:11:22:33:44:55). Real NICs ship with manufacturer-assigned OUIs; these values are unmistakable PoC artifacts. Rationale: Both MAC addresses are explicit IOCs from Palo Alto Networks' bundle and have OUIs that no real NIC manufacturer owns — aa:bb:cc and 00:11:22 are classic documentation/placeholder values used in the PoC client spoofing. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/palo-alto-warns-of-active-exploitation.html
ATT&CKT1133 T1036
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal pentester using a tool that doesn't randomise MACs and ships with the same documentation defaults
  • Network engineer running GlobalProtect from a Hyper-V/VirtualBox guest whose virtual NIC was assigned a manually-typed placeholder MAC during lab setup
  • Asset-management or HIP-misconfiguration where the agent fails to read the real MAC and falls back to a default
  • Threat-research VM in your environment that emulates the PoC client for IOC validation
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the SourceIP, SourceUserName and timestamp for each hit. Confirm whether the same session also reported the PoC OS string or one of the cookie-cutter hostnames — multiple PoC indicators together is near-certain exploitation. 2) Contain: terminate the GP session, disable the account, block the source public IP, and force a credential reset. 3) Hunt: search 90 days for any other sessions reporting these MACs against any account; pivot on the public_ip to find sibling sessions; correlate against the PAN advisory for newer IOCs and confirm the appliance is patched against CVE-2026-0257.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DeviceVendor has 'Palo Alto'
| where Message has_any ('aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff', '00:11:22:33:44:55')
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DeviceAction, Activity, SourceMACAddress, DestinationMACAddress, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-0257")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-0257")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

| where AccountName !endswith "$"

| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)

| where Account !endswith "$"

| order by TimeGenerated desc

status: experimental
description: |

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02

    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access

    category: process_creation
    product: windows

        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'

   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"

Critical

Critical Splunk Enterprise Flaw Lets Attackers Run Code Without Authentication

The Hacker News
2026-06-13 12 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Splunk has released security updates to address a critical security flaw in Splunk Enterprise that could be exploited to conduct unauthenticated file operations and even remote code execution. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-20253, is rated 9.8 on the CVSS scoring system. "In Splunk Enterprise versions below 10.2.4 and 10.0.7, an unauthenticated user could create or truncate arbitrary
