Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("6144d433f8a0316869877b5f834c801251bbb936e5f1577c5680878c7443c98b", "42b59fdbe1b72895b2951412222ebf40") or SHA1 in~ ("6144d433f8a0316869877b5f834c801251bbb936e5f1577c5680878c7443c98b", "42b59fdbe1b72895b2951412222ebf40") or MD5 in~ ("6144d433f8a0316869877b5f834c801251bbb936e5f1577c5680878c7443c98b", "42b59fdbe1b72895b2951412222ebf40")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("6144d433f8a0316869877b5f834c801251bbb936e5f1577c5680878c7443c98b", "42b59fdbe1b72895b2951412222ebf40") or SHA1 in~ ("6144d433f8a0316869877b5f834c801251bbb936e5f1577c5680878c7443c98b", "42b59fdbe1b72895b2951412222ebf40") or MD5 in~ ("6144d433f8a0316869877b5f834c801251bbb936e5f1577c5680878c7443c98b", "42b59fdbe1b72895b2951412222ebf40")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["6144d433f8a0316869877b5f834c801251bbb936e5f1577c5680878c7443c98b", "42b59fdbe1b72895b2951412222ebf40"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → OAuth consent / suspicious app grant

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB

| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web

    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)

              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;

// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:

let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host

    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/

    category: process_creation

            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'

            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'

falsepositives:

level: high

| where Result =~ "success"

         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result

Budibase: POST to /api/public/v1/roles/assign (CVE-2026-48150 exploit endpoint) AIExploitation High
Hunts the specific exploit URL path /api/public/v1/roles/assign on Budibase instances. This endpoint is the controller named in CVE-2026-48150 where workspace-scoped builders mass-assign builder:true or admin:true to escalate to global admin. Any POST with a 200 response on a pre-3.39.0 build is suspect. Rationale: The URL path /api/public/v1/roles/assign is the literal controller endpoint named in the advisory (packages/server/src/api/controllers/public/roles.ts:13-17). Any POST + 2xx on a pre-3.39.0 build is the in-the-wild exploit shape from Alice's curl in the PoC. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6xp4-cf37-ppjh • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-48150
ATT&CKT1190 T1068
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Enterprise admin scripting bulk user role grants via the public API after patching
  • Internal SecOps replaying historical traffic against a staging instance
  • Budibase platform-engineering team running smoke tests post-deploy
  • Security scanner (Burp/ZAP/nuclei) hitting the endpoint as part of authorised pentest
  • Vulnerability-scanner endpoint enumeration confirming 401/403 vs 200
Suppression filter
| where User !in~ ("svc-budibase-admin","platform-engineering@corp.local")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm Budibase server version — if >= 3.39.0 the vuln is patched and the call is admin-legitimate. Pull the request body from WAF/proxy and check whether `builder:true` or `admin:true` is at the JSON root. Cross-reference the calling API key's owner in Budibase global users — they should already be a global admin. Step 2 (contain): If exploit is confirmed, revoke the offending API key via /api/global/self/api_key delete, force-reset the actor account, and revert any privilege grants logged in Budibase audit after the request. Snapshot the Budibase couchdb for forensics. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the actor's account-id across the prior 30 days for /api/global/self/api_key mints, all /api/public/v1/* calls, and any prior workspace-scoped role assignments. Search Budibase audit for downstream datasource/automation/SCIM changes by the same actor.
// Defender Advanced Hunting picks up outbound calls only when the attacker uses a Windows endpoint with curl/python to hit the Budibase API
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has "/api/public/v1/roles/assign"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("curl.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","node.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
// Budibase fronted by Azure App Service / IIS / reverse-proxy — pick the table that fits your deployment.
// (1) Azure App Service
AppServiceHTTPLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where CsMethod == "POST"
| where CsUriStem has "/api/public/v1/roles/assign"
| where ScStatus in (200,201)
| project TimeGenerated, BudibaseHost=CsHost, ClientIP=CIp, User=CsUsername, UserAgent, CsUriStem, ScStatus
| union (
// (2) IIS-hosted Budibase
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csMethod == "POST"
| where csUriStem has "/api/public/v1/roles/assign"
| where scStatus in (200,201)
| project TimeGenerated, BudibaseHost=Computer, ClientIP=cIP, User=csUserName, UserAgent=csUserAgent, CsUriStem=csUriStem, ScStatus=scStatus
)
| union (
// (3) WAF / reverse-proxy (CEF)
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestMethod == "POST"
| where RequestURL has "/api/public/v1/roles/assign"
| project TimeGenerated, BudibaseHost=DestinationHostName, ClientIP=SourceIP, User=SourceUserName, UserAgent=RequestClientApplication, CsUriStem=RequestURL, ScStatus=tolong(EventOutcome)
)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Budibase: Workspace-scoped builder mints public API key via /api/global/self/api_key AIWeaponization Medium
Hunts GET /api/global/self/api_key calls — the precursor step in the PoC where Alice (a workspace-scoped builder) mints an API key tied to her identity so she can then call the public-API exploit endpoint. Without this key, the /api/public/v1/roles/assign call is impossible. Rationale: Step 2 of the PoC: `curl -sS -b alice "$BASE/api/global/self/api_key"`. Workspace-scoped builders should rarely need a public-API key — they build inside the UI. A mint by a non-global-admin is the precursor signal that proceeds to the exploit POST. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6xp4-cf37-ppjh
ATT&CKT1098 T1550.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate global admin minting their own API key for automation tooling
  • Budibase developer rotating their personal API key after a planned rotation window
  • CI/CD pipeline that uses a service-account global admin to generate keys for integration tests
  • Internal SCIM provisioning automation that calls /api/global/self/api_key
  • Workspace builder legitimately granted public-API access for a specific business workflow
Suppression filter
| where User !in~ ("svc-budibase-admin","platform-engineering@corp.local","ci-budibase@corp.local")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Look up the actor's user record in Budibase global users and confirm their `builder.global` and `admin.global` flags. If both are unset (workspace-scoped builder), this mint is anomalous — the public API is designed for global identities. Step 2 (contain): Revoke the minted API key via the global-users API. Notify the user out-of-band to confirm whether they initiated the mint legitimately. Step 3 (hunt): Within the next 60 minutes after the mint, query for POST calls to /api/public/v1/* from the same client IP and from any request bearing x-budibase-api-key. Any POST to /roles/assign is a confirmed exploit chain.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has "/api/global/self/api_key"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("curl.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","node.exe","wget.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP
| order by Timestamp desc
AppServiceHTTPLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where CsMethod == "GET"
| where CsUriStem has "/api/global/self/api_key"
| where ScStatus == 200
| project TimeGenerated, BudibaseHost=CsHost, ClientIP=CIp, User=CsUsername, UserAgent, CsUriStem
| union (
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csMethod == "GET"
| where csUriStem has "/api/global/self/api_key"
| where scStatus == 200
| project TimeGenerated, BudibaseHost=Computer, ClientIP=cIP, User=csUserName, UserAgent=csUserAgent, CsUriStem=csUriStem
)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Budibase API Key Self-Mint
id: 7a1d2e4c-9b5f-4c8e-a3d1-2e6f9c8b7d4a

references:

  condition: selection
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate Budibase developer minting an API key for automation
level: medium
(source:azure.appservice OR source:nginx OR source:iis OR source:apache) (@http.method:GET OR @method:GET) @http.url_details.path:*/api/global/self/api_key* @http.status_code:200
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Web.url) as url values(Web.user) as user values(Web.status) as status from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*/api/global/self/api_key*" Web.http_method=GET Web.status=200 by Web.dest Web.src Web.user Web.http_user_agent | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | rename dest as budibase_host, src as client_ip

Budibase: API-key mint quickly followed by /api/public/v1/roles/assign POST (CVE-2026-48150 chain) AIExploitation High
Temporal correlation of the exact PoC sequence: a GET to /api/global/self/api_key (key mint) followed within 10 minutes by a POST to /api/public/v1/roles/assign from the same client IP / user. This is the in-the-wild attack chain reconstructed from the advisory. Rationale: Reconstructs the exact PoC sequence from the advisory: Step 2 mints the API key, Step 3 fires the exploit POST. The 10-minute window matches typical curl-pasted attack tempo and is narrow enough to exclude legitimate same-day re-use. Multi-event temporal correlation = no Sigma. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6xp4-cf37-ppjh
ATT&CKT1190 T1068 T1098
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin scripting bulk role grants right after rotating their own API key
  • Pentester running the documented PoC against staging
  • Automated integration test mints key then exercises public API endpoints
  • CI pipeline that always mints fresh keys before role-management operations
  • Vulnerability scanner using known PoCs
Suppression filter
| where MintUser !in~ ("svc-budibase-admin","platform-engineering@corp.local","ci-budibase@corp.local")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the user identity tied to the source IP from Budibase auth logs at the mint time — workspace-scoped builder = high confidence exploit, global admin = likely admin-legitimate. Capture the POST body (from WAF if available) and look for `builder:true` / `admin:true` at the JSON root. Step 2 (contain): Revoke the minted API key, disable the actor's user, and reset any users that appear in the userIds array of the POST body — those are the privilege-grant targets. Step 3 (hunt): Audit `builder.global=true` and `admin.global=true` user-doc transitions in Budibase couchdb across the prior 7 days. Look for follow-on actions by the newly-elevated identities: datasource credential reads, SCIM config changes, OIDC client edits.
let WindowMinutes = 10m;
let Mint = DeviceNetworkEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
  | where RemoteUrl has "/api/global/self/api_key"
  | project MintTime=Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, MintCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, MintUrl=RemoteUrl, MintIP=RemoteIP;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has "/api/public/v1/roles/assign"
| join kind=inner Mint on DeviceId
| where Timestamp between (MintTime .. MintTime + WindowMinutes)
| project MintTime, ExploitTime=Timestamp, DelaySec=datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, MintTime), DeviceName, AccountName, MintCmd, ExploitCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ExploitUrl=RemoteUrl, MintIP
| order by ExploitTime desc
let WindowMinutes = 10m;
let Mint = AppServiceHTTPLogs
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where CsMethod == "GET"
  | where CsUriStem has "/api/global/self/api_key"
  | where ScStatus == 200
  | project MintTime=TimeGenerated, ClientIP=CIp, MintUser=CsUsername, MintHost=CsHost;
AppServiceHTTPLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where CsMethod == "POST"
| where CsUriStem has "/api/public/v1/roles/assign"
| where ScStatus in (200,201)
| project ExploitTime=TimeGenerated, ClientIP=CIp, ExploitUser=CsUsername, ExploitHost=CsHost, ExploitUserAgent=UserAgent, ExploitUri=CsUriStem
| join kind=inner Mint on ClientIP
| where ExploitTime between (MintTime .. MintTime + WindowMinutes)
| extend DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', ExploitTime, MintTime)
| project MintTime, ExploitTime, DelaySec, ClientIP, MintUser, ExploitUser, ExploitHost, ExploitUserAgent, ExploitUri

Budibase: roles/assign POST body containing builder:true or admin:true (mass-assignment) AIExploitation High
Hunts the mass-assignment payload itself — POST bodies to /api/public/v1/roles/assign that contain `builder:true` or `admin:true` at the JSON root. The advisory shows the controller spreads the body straight into the SDK call, so these root-level flags are the exploitation primitive (CWE-915). Rationale: The advisory shows the body keys `builder` and `admin` flow directly into the SDK — `if (opts.builder) user.builder = { global: true }`. Catching either flag at the JSON root in a POST to this exact path is the highest-fidelity primitive available; requires WAF/proxy body capture, which is typical in enterprise Budibase deployments fronted by Azure App Gateway / Cloudflare / F5. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6xp4-cf37-ppjh • https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/915.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1068
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Patched 3.39.0+ instance where a global admin legitimately uses the public API to grant builder/admin scope
  • Internal tooling that scripts role grants via the public API as part of provisioning
  • Pentester running the documented advisory PoC against staging
  • WAF/proxy replaying historical traffic to a dev instance
  • Body capture firing on the literal advisory PoC examples committed to internal docs
Suppression filter
| where User !in~ ("svc-budibase-admin","platform-engineering@corp.local")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the actor identity from the API key in the x-budibase-api-key header. Check Budibase global-users couchdb for that account's `builder.global` and `admin.global` at the time of the request — if either was already true, this is admin-legitimate. Step 2 (contain): Revoke the API key. Snapshot the request body and the userIds array — every id in that array is a victim of privilege escalation. Restore each victim's prior role from couchdb backup or audit log. Step 3 (hunt): Identify newly-elevated user-ids across the prior 30 days by diffing user docs. Audit any actions taken by those identities post-elevation: datasource credential views, automation edits, SCIM/OIDC config touches, /api/global/users/* writes.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestMethod == "POST"
| where RequestURL has "/api/public/v1/roles/assign"
| where Message has_any ("\"builder\":true","\"admin\":true","\"builder\": true","\"admin\": true")
| project TimeGenerated, BudibaseHost=DestinationHostName, ClientIP=SourceIP, User=SourceUserName, UserAgent=RequestClientApplication, RequestURL, BodySnippet=substring(Message,0,500)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Budibase: workspace-scoped builder transitions to builder.global=true (audit-log signal) AIInstallation High
Hunts the privilege state-change itself in Budibase couchdb / audit logs — a user whose document was `builder.apps:[app_...]` with `builder.global:false` flips to `builder.global:true`, or whose `admin.global:false` flips to `true`. This is the post-condition the SDK applies and the ground-truth signal regardless of which API path was abused. Rationale: The advisory shows the SDK writes `user.builder = { global: true }` and `user.admin = { global: true }` directly. Hunting this state transition in Budibase audit/couchdb logs is the highest-confidence ground-truth detection — it catches the exploit regardless of whether the attacker used /api/public/v1/roles/assign or any other endpoint that shares the broken middleware. Reviewer-requested correlation of role-before vs role-after. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6xp4-cf37-ppjh
ATT&CKT1098 T1068
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Global admin legitimately granting global builder/admin scope to a new hire
  • SCIM provisioning automation setting global flags on imported users
  • Initial Budibase setup where the first admin self-promotes
  • Backup-restore replay re-asserting role state during DR drill
  • Role-rotation playbook bumping a temporary admin
Suppression filter
| where SyslogMessage !has "actor_role=admin.global"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the actor (caller) and the target user. Confirm the actor was a global admin BEFORE the change — if the actor's prior state was workspace-scoped builder, this is the CVE-2026-48150 exploit. Pull the corresponding HTTP request (correlated by request-id or timestamp) and inspect the POST body. Step 2 (contain): Revert the target user's `builder` / `admin` field to its prior value via couchdb. Disable the actor account and revoke all its API keys. Step 3 (hunt): Within the same time window, enumerate every Budibase user whose `builder.global` or `admin.global` flipped to true. Each is a potentially-attacker-controlled global admin. Audit datasource credentials, automation edits, and SCIM/OIDC config changes by all newly-elevated identities.

| project TimeGenerated, BudibaseHost=HostName, Facility, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

China-Linked Hackers Backdoored Linux Login Software to Hide for Nearly a Decade

The Hacker News
2026-06-12 11 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Instead of hiding on the laptops and servers defenders watch most closely, a China-nexus group spent close to a decade hidden inside the Linux login system itself. Sygnia, which tracks the group as Velvet Ant, says it backdoored the PAM and OpenSSH components that decide who is allowed to sign in, planting its access where ordinary cleanup could not reach it. Unauthorized write to Linux PAM authentication module (pam_unix.so swap) AIInstallation High
Detects file creation/modification of pam_unix.so (or sibling PAM modules) by any process other than the system package manager. Velvet Ant's Operation Highland replaced this exact module with 9 backdoored builds that accepted a magic password and logged real credentials — direct swap is the highest-fidelity persistence pivot in the campaign. Rationale: Article + Sygnia blog explicitly name pam_unix.so as the swapped module with 9 backdoored variants discovered. File-write to canonical PAM module paths by a non-package-manager process is a direct hit on the documented TTP and effectively unfalsifiable without legitimate package activity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sygnia.co/blog/operation-highland-velvet-ant/ • https://www.scworld.com/brief/china-nexus-group-hid-in-linux-login-system-for-nearly-a-decade
ATT&CKT1556.003 T1554
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Distro security update outside the maintained package-manager allowlist (e.g. manually invoked 'install' on a downloaded .deb via curl|sh)
  • Configuration management agent (Ansible/Salt/Puppet) deploying a custom or in-house PAM module under a non-standard process name
  • Container-image build process writing PAM modules during image construction
  • System administrator manually reinstalling pam package via 'apt-get install --reinstall' under sudo from interactive shell
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("ansible","salt-minion","puppet","chef-client","cfengine") and not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("--reinstall","makepkg","rpmbuild"))
Response runbook
1) Triage — extract SHA256 of the written .so; compare against distro package hash via 'rpm -V pam' or 'dpkg --verify libpam-modules'; review process tree of InitiatingProcessFileName and its parent; check whether the host had a sanctioned change window. 2) Contain — isolate the host; snapshot /lib*/security/ and /etc/pam.d/ for forensics; revoke and rotate every credential used to SSH to or sudo on the host within the lookback (article: credentials captured at login). 3) Hunt — fan out the SHA256 across the Linux fleet; pull sshd and ssh binary hashes from the same host; hunt outbound DNS/TCP from sshd-context processes for any kill-switch beacon.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FolderPath has_any (@"/lib/security/", @"/lib64/security/", @"/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/security/", @"/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/security/", @"/usr/lib64/security/")
| where FileName startswith "pam_" and FileName endswith ".so"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("dpkg","dpkg-deb","apt","apt-get","aptitude","unattended-upgrade","yum","dnf","rpm","zypper","pacman","ldconfig","snapd","snap")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, MD5, PreviousFileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/lib/security/","/lib64/security/","/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/security/","/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/security/","/usr/lib64/security/")
| where TargetFileName startswith "pam_" and TargetFileName endswith ".so"
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("dpkg","dpkg-deb","apt","apt-get","aptitude","unattended-upgrade","yum","dnf","rpm","zypper","pacman","ldconfig","snapd","snap")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Unauthorized modification of OpenSSH sshd or ssh client binary AIInstallation High
Detects write or replacement of the canonical OpenSSH binaries (/usr/sbin/sshd, /usr/bin/ssh) outside of package-manager updates. Operation Highland modified these binaries to log credentials and every command typed with a hidden switch to silence logging, making any uncontrolled write to them campaign-defining. Rationale: Article + Sygnia state sshd/ssh were altered to log credentials and typed commands with a hidden disable switch. Detecting file writes to the canonical OpenSSH paths by anything other than the package manager is a direct, low-FP hit on the documented persistence method. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sygnia.co/blog/operation-highland-velvet-ant/ • https://www.scworld.com/brief/china-nexus-group-hid-in-linux-login-system-for-nearly-a-decade
ATT&CKT1554 T1556 T1056.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • openssh-server package upgrade run through a wrapper (e.g. unattended-upgrade not present, security-update.sh script invokes apt)
  • Hardened-build pipeline replacing distro openssh with an internally compiled binary deployed via Ansible/Salt
  • Container image bake writing sshd into a layer at build time
  • Manual 'apt-get install --reinstall openssh-server' by a sysadmin under interactive sudo
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("ansible","salt-minion","puppet","chef-client","cfengine") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "--reinstall"
Response runbook
1) Triage — pull SHA256 of new sshd/ssh; compare to distro package hash ('dpkg-query -W -f=' then 'apt-cache' or 'rpm -qf'); check for a hidden config flag (e.g. extra env var or stat-suppressed sibling file) and grep strings for unexpected log paths. 2) Contain — isolate host; capture binary + memory; restore sshd from a verified distro mirror; kill all active sshd sessions; force rotation of every SSH credential used against the host plus any key material loaded by users that logged in since modification. 3) Hunt — fleet-wide hash search for the same SHA256 on sshd, ssh, ssh-keygen, scp, sftp; cross-check pam_unix.so on the same host (Velvet Ant typically modifies both); review auth log gaps and any sshd outbound connections.

id: e0a9b2c1-3f47-4c2c-9e0b-2f1d4a9b1e22
status: experimental
description: Detects write/replacement of /usr/sbin/sshd or /usr/bin/ssh by any process other than the host package manager. Maps to Sygnia Velvet Ant Operation Highland — actor swapped OpenSSH binaries to log credentials and every command typed.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/china-linked-hackers-backdoored-linux.html
  - https://www.sygnia.co/blog/operation-highland-velvet-ant/
author: thn-usecases
date: 2026/06/13
tags:
  - attack.persistence
  - attack.t1554
  - attack.t1556
  - attack.credential_access
logsource:
  product: linux
  category: file_event
detection:
  selection:
    TargetFilename:
      - '/usr/sbin/sshd'
      - '/usr/bin/sshd'
      - '/usr/bin/ssh'
      - '/usr/sbin/ssh'
      - '/usr/bin/ssh-keygen'
      - '/usr/bin/scp'
      - '/usr/bin/sftp'
  filter_pkgmgr:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/dpkg'
      - '/dpkg-deb'
      - '/apt'
      - '/apt-get'
      - '/unattended-upgrade'
      - '/yum'
      - '/dnf'
      - '/rpm'
      - '/zypper'
      - '/pacman'
      - '/snapd'
  condition: selection and not filter_pkgmgr
falsepositives:
  - openssh-server package upgrade via a non-allowlisted wrapper
  - In-house compiled OpenSSH deployed by configuration management
level: high
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:(PATH OR SYSCALL) @file.path:(/usr/sbin/sshd OR /usr/bin/sshd OR /usr/bin/ssh OR /usr/sbin/ssh OR /usr/bin/ssh-keygen OR /usr/bin/scp OR /usr/bin/sftp OR /usr/bin/ssh-agent) -@process.executable.path:(*/dpkg* OR */apt* OR */apt-get* OR */yum* OR */dnf* OR */rpm* OR */zypper* OR */pacman* OR */unattended-upgrade* OR */snapd*)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/^\/(usr\/sbin\/sshd|usr\/bin\/sshd|usr\/bin\/ssh|usr\/sbin\/ssh|usr\/bin\/ssh-keygen|usr\/bin\/scp|usr\/bin\/sftp|usr\/bin\/ssh-agent)$/i
| NOT ContextImageFileName=/\/(dpkg|dpkg-deb|apt|apt-get|unattended-upgrade|yum|dnf|rpm|zypper|pacman|snapd)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, TargetFileName, ContextImageFileName, UserName], function=count())
| count > 0
ENDPOINT

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Filesystem.file_path) as file_path values(Filesystem.file_hash) as file_hash values(Filesystem.process_name) as process_name values(Filesystem.user) as user from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_path IN ("/usr/sbin/sshd","/usr/bin/sshd","/usr/bin/ssh","/usr/sbin/ssh","/usr/bin/ssh-keygen","/usr/bin/scp","/usr/bin/sftp") Filesystem.action IN ("created","modified","renamed") NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("dpkg","dpkg-deb","apt","apt-get","unattended-upgrade","yum","dnf","rpm","zypper","pacman") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | sort 0 - lastTime
sshd writing to non-standard files (credential-capture log artifact) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the sshd process writing to file paths outside its expected runtime set (PID file, audit/syslog sockets, sftp transfer targets). The Operation Highland sshd backdoor recorded every credential and typed command to a hidden file; any file-write originating from sshd to /tmp, /var/tmp, /dev/shm, /etc, or a non-standard path under /var is the artefact. Rationale: Article: Operation Highland sshd 'logging credentials and every command typed, with a hidden switch to turn that logging off when needed.' The capture file has to land somewhere on disk. sshd's expected write set is small (PID, syslog forwards, user .ssh, sftp transfers) — anything else from sshd is a credential-capture candidate. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sygnia.co/blog/operation-highland-velvet-ant/
ATT&CKT1056.001 T1003.008 T1556.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • sftp-internal subsystem inside sshd writing user-uploaded files to non-/home destinations
  • PAM session module writing motd/lastlog timestamps via sshd context to a vendor-custom path
  • Container-friendly sshd builds that write a runtime socket to /tmp under a non-standard name
  • Custom sshd ChrootDirectory configurations placing user data outside /home
  • Local PAM module from an EDR/UEBA agent writing audit breadcrumbs into /var/lib/<vendor>/
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath startswith "/var/lib/" and FolderPath has_any ("crowdstrike","sentinelone","defender","qualys","rapid7"))
Response runbook
1) Triage — read the written file (cat / xxd first bytes) to confirm credential-style content (usernames, plaintext passwords, typed commands); cross-check sshd binary SHA256 against the distro package. 2) Contain — isolate host; copy and quarantine the capture file for forensics; replace sshd from verified package source; force password + key rotation for every account that authenticated to the host since the file's first-seen timestamp. 3) Hunt — pivot on the file path across the Linux fleet; check for matching pam_unix.so anomalies; review egress from sshd-context to identify out-of-band exfil of the capture file.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "sshd"
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath in~ ("/usr/sbin/","/usr/bin/")
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where not (FolderPath in~ ("/var/run/","/run/","/var/log/","/var/empty/sshd/","/var/lib/sss/") )
| where not (FolderPath startswith "/home/" and FolderPath contains "/.ssh/")
| where not (FolderPath startswith "/root/.ssh/")
| where not (FolderPath startswith "/tmp/ssh-")
| where FileName !in~ ("sshd.pid","auth.log","secure","lastlog","wtmp","btmp","utmp")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, FileSize, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RequestAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName =~ "sshd"
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where not (TargetFilePath startswith "/var/run/" or TargetFilePath startswith "/run/" or TargetFilePath startswith "/var/log/" or TargetFilePath startswith "/var/empty/sshd/" or TargetFilePath startswith "/var/lib/sss/")
| where not (TargetFilePath startswith "/home/" and TargetFilePath contains "/.ssh/")
| where not (TargetFilePath startswith "/root/.ssh/")
| where not (TargetFilePath startswith "/tmp/ssh-")
| where TargetFileName !in~ ("sshd.pid","auth.log","secure","lastlog","wtmp","btmp","utmp")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSize, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:(PATH OR SYSCALL) @process.executable.path:(/usr/sbin/sshd OR /usr/bin/sshd) @auditd.syscall:(open OR openat OR write OR creat OR rename) -@file.path:(/var/run/sshd.pid OR /run/sshd.pid OR /var/log/auth.log OR /var/log/secure OR /var/log/wtmp OR /var/log/btmp OR /var/log/lastlog OR /var/log/utmp OR /var/empty/sshd/* OR /home/*/.ssh/* OR /root/.ssh/* OR /tmp/ssh-* OR /var/lib/sss/*)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten ContextImageFileName=/\/(usr\/sbin|usr\/bin)\/sshd$/i
| NOT TargetFileName=/\/(var\/run\/sshd\.pid|run\/sshd\.pid|var\/log\/(auth\.log|secure|wtmp|btmp|lastlog|utmp)|home\/[^\/]+\/\.ssh\/.*|root\/\.ssh\/.*|tmp\/ssh-.*|var\/empty\/sshd\/.*|var\/lib\/sss\/.*)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, TargetFileName, UserName], function=count())
| count > 0
ENDPOINT

| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Filesystem.file_path) as file_path values(Filesystem.file_name) as file_name from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.process_name="sshd" Filesystem.action IN ("created","modified") NOT (Filesystem.file_path IN ("/var/run/sshd.pid","/run/sshd.pid","/var/log/auth.log","/var/log/secure","/var/log/lastlog","/var/log/wtmp","/var/log/btmp","/var/log/utmp","/run/utmp","/var/empty/sshd") OR Filesystem.file_path="/home/*/.ssh/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="/root/.ssh/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="/tmp/ssh-*" OR Filesystem.file_path="/var/lib/sss/*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | sort 0 - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Filesystem.file_path) as file_path values(Filesystem.file_name) as file_name from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.process_name="sshd" Filesystem.action IN ("created","modified") NOT (Filesystem.file_path IN ("/var/run/sshd.pid","/run/sshd.pid","/var/log/auth.log","/var/log/secure","/var/log/lastlog","/var/log/wtmp","/var/log/btmp","/var/log/utmp","/run/utmp","/var/empty/sshd") OR Filesystem.file_path="/home/*/.ssh/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="/root/.ssh/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="/tmp/ssh-*" OR Filesystem.file_path="/var/lib/sss/*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | sort 0 - lastTime
Internet-facing web service spawning interactive SSH into management subnet AIDelivery High
Detects a web server process (httpd, nginx, apache2, tomcat, php-fpm, node, java app server) spawning ssh/scp/sftp/sshpass to an internal RFC1918 destination — the exact pivot Sygnia attributes to Operation Highland, where an internet-facing web server was used as a bridge to open remote sessions deep inside an air-gapped segment. Rationale: Article: 'used other disguised tools and an internet-facing web server as a bridge, passing commands through it to open remote sessions deep inside the segment that had no direct internet access.' A web-server parent spawning ssh/scp/sftp/socat at all is rare in production; targeting RFC1918 makes it the pivot signature. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sygnia.co/blog/operation-highland-velvet-ant/ • https://www.scworld.com/brief/china-nexus-group-hid-in-linux-login-system-for-nearly-a-decade
ATT&CKT1190 T1133 T1021.004 T1090.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • CI/CD agent embedded in a web tier (e.g. Jenkins runner under tomcat) legitimately scp-ing build artefacts to internal hosts
  • Deploy hook in a PHP app calling 'ssh deploy@internal' as part of release automation
  • Healthcheck plugin shelling 'nc -zv internal-db 5432' from haproxy
  • Log-shipping script invoked from nginx error handler that uses scp to push debug bundles
  • Backup wrapper inside a java app server initiating scp to an internal backup target
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("jenkins","deploy","gitlab-runner","awx","rundeck") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("deploy","backup","rsync")
Response runbook
1) Triage — pull the web server access log for the same minute and identify the request path that triggered the spawn (webshell signature); inspect the SSH destination IP and the credential/key used; check whether the web server has a documented automation parent. 2) Contain — kill active ssh/socat session; block egress from web tier to management subnet at host firewall; quarantine any webshell artefact found in the web root; rotate keys/passwords for the target account. 3) Hunt — fan-out same parent→child pairing across other internet-facing hosts; pivot on the destination internal IP to identify what the attacker reached; check the destination for pam_unix.so / sshd hash anomalies.
let WebParents = dynamic(["httpd","nginx","apache2","tomcat","java","node","php-fpm","php-cgi","uwsgi","gunicorn","caddy","lighttpd","haproxy"]);
let PivotTools = dynamic(["ssh","sshpass","scp","sftp","plink","autossh","socat","ncat","nc"]);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (WebParents)
| where FileName in~ (PivotTools)
| extend RfcTarget = extract(@"(?:^|\s)(?:-[a-zA-Z]\s+)?(?:[A-Za-z0-9_\-]+@)?((?:10\.|172\.(?:1[6-9]|2[0-9]|3[01])\.|192\.168\.)\d+\.\d+\.\d+|(?:10\.|172\.(?:1[6-9]|2[0-9]|3[01])\.|192\.168\.)[0-9.]+)", 1, ProcessCommandLine)
| where isnotempty(RfcTarget) or ProcessCommandLine has_any (".internal",".corp",".local",".lan",".intranet")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, RfcTarget, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
let WebParents = dynamic(["httpd","nginx","apache2","tomcat","java","node","php-fpm","php-cgi","uwsgi","gunicorn","caddy","lighttpd","haproxy"]);
let PivotTools = dynamic(["ssh","sshpass","scp","sftp","plink","autossh","socat","ncat","nc"]);
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName in~ (WebParents)
| where ActingProcessName in~ (PivotTools)
| extend RfcTarget = extract(@"(?:^|\s)(?:-[a-zA-Z]\s+)?(?:[A-Za-z0-9_\-]+@)?((?:10\.|172\.(?:1[6-9]|2[0-9]|3[01])\.|192\.168\.)[0-9.]+)", 1, ActingProcessCommandLine)
| where isnotempty(RfcTarget) or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (".internal",".corp",".local",".lan",".intranet")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, RfcTarget
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Web Server Process Spawns SSH or Tunnel Tool Targeting RFC1918
id: 4c2b8f9a-1d1d-4e83-b1a9-9cb4cdbc8a91
status: experimental
description: Detects an internet-facing web server (httpd/nginx/tomcat/php-fpm/etc.) spawning ssh, scp, sftp, sshpass, autossh, socat, or ncat. Maps to Sygnia Velvet Ant Operation Highland — actor used an internet-facing web server as the bridge into an isolated network segment.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/china-linked-hackers-backdoored-linux.html
  - https://www.sygnia.co/blog/operation-highland-velvet-ant/
author: thn-usecases
date: 2026/06/13
tags:
  - attack.initial_access
  - attack.lateral_movement
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.t1021.004
  - attack.t1090.001
logsource:
  product: linux
  category: process_creation
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '/httpd'
      - '/nginx'
      - '/apache2'
      - '/tomcat'
      - '/java'
      - '/node'
      - '/php-fpm'
      - '/php-cgi'
      - '/uwsgi'
      - '/gunicorn'
      - '/caddy'
      - '/lighttpd'
      - '/haproxy'
  selection_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/ssh'
      - '/sshpass'
      - '/scp'
      - '/sftp'
      - '/plink'
      - '/autossh'
      - '/socat'
      - '/ncat'
      - '/nc'
  condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
  - Application-defined deploy hooks that legitimately invoke ssh/scp from a web tier
  - Healthcheck plugin shelling out to test SSH reachability
level: high
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.parent.name:(httpd OR nginx OR apache2 OR tomcat OR java OR node OR php-fpm OR php-cgi OR uwsgi OR gunicorn OR caddy OR lighttpd OR haproxy) @process.name:(ssh OR sshpass OR scp OR sftp OR plink OR autossh OR socat OR ncat OR nc) (@process.command_line:*10.* OR @process.command_line:*172.16.* OR @process.command_line:*172.17.* OR @process.command_line:*172.18.* OR @process.command_line:*172.19.* OR @process.command_line:*172.2* OR @process.command_line:*172.30.* OR @process.command_line:*172.31.* OR @process.command_line:*192.168.* OR @process.command_line:*.internal* OR @process.command_line:*.corp* OR @process.command_line:*.local* OR @process.command_line:*.lan*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/^(httpd|nginx|apache2|tomcat|java|node|php-fpm|php-cgi|uwsgi|gunicorn|caddy|lighttpd|haproxy)$/i ImageFileName=/\/(ssh|sshpass|scp|sftp|plink|autossh|socat|ncat|nc)$/i
| regex("(10\\.|172\\.(1[6-9]|2[0-9]|3[01])\\.|192\\.168\\.|\\.internal|\\.corp|\\.local|\\.lan|\\.intranet)", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, UserName], function=count())
ENDPOINT

| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as process values(Processes.process_path) as process_path from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("httpd","nginx","apache2","tomcat","java","node","php-fpm","php-cgi","uwsgi","gunicorn","caddy","haproxy","lighttpd") Processes.process_name IN ("ssh","sshpass","scp","sftp","plink","autossh","socat","ncat","nc") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | sort 0 - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as process values(Processes.process_path) as process_path from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("httpd","nginx","apache2","tomcat","java","node","php-fpm","php-cgi","uwsgi","gunicorn","caddy","haproxy","lighttpd") Processes.process_name IN ("ssh","sshpass","scp","sftp","plink","autossh","socat","ncat","nc") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | sort 0 - lastTime
First-seen pam_unix.so / sshd / ssh binary hash in Linux fleet AIInstallation Medium
Anti-baseline hunting query: surfaces SHA256 values of pam_unix.so, sshd, ssh, scp, sftp that appear in the recent window but were never observed in the 60-day baseline. Velvet Ant built 9 distinct compile-variants of pam_unix.so per host — a fresh hash on a long-stable binary is the canonical indicator regardless of how it got there. Rationale: Article + Sygnia: 9 distinct compile-variants of pam_unix.so per Operation Highland host. Hash-anti-baseline catches the variant regardless of write path; works even when the swap predates monitoring (because the new hash will eventually appear in execution/load telemetry). Cross-checked against: • https://www.sygnia.co/blog/operation-highland-velvet-ant/ • https://www.scworld.com/brief/china-nexus-group-hid-in-linux-login-system-for-nearly-a-decade
ATT&CKT1554 T1556.003 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Distro security update introducing a new openssh-server build (legitimate new hash, fleet-wide)
  • Newly onboarded host running a different distro version not present in baseline
  • libpam-modules upgrade pushing a new pam_unix.so build
  • In-house custom-compiled OpenSSH rollout under a change ticket
  • Hardened-image refresh from golden image producing new but legitimate hashes
Suppression filter
| where not (FirstSeen > ago(48h) and HostCount > 100)
Response runbook
1) Triage — correlate the new hash against the package metadata on the host ('rpm -V', 'dpkg -V libpam-modules openssh-server') and against the distro vendor's signed package hash; if the hash is unaccounted for, treat as suspect. 2) Contain — isolate the host; preserve binary + memory; restore from verified package mirror; rotate credentials used since the binary first appeared. 3) Hunt — pivot on the unaccounted hash across the fleet to find all infected hosts; cross-check whether the same hosts also have anomalous sshd or pam_unix.so; review egress from those hosts during their first-seen window.
let Lookback = 60d;
let Recent = 7d;
let AuthBinaries = dynamic(["sshd","ssh","scp","sftp","ssh-keygen","ssh-agent"]);
let BaselineExec = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp between (ago(Lookback) .. ago(Recent))
    | where FileName in~ (AuthBinaries) and FolderPath in~ ("/usr/sbin/","/usr/bin/")
    | summarize by SHA256, FileName;
let RecentExec = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(Recent)
    | where FileName in~ (AuthBinaries) and FolderPath in~ ("/usr/sbin/","/usr/bin/")
    | summarize FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), HostCount = dcount(DeviceId), AnyHost = any(DeviceName), AnyCmd = any(ProcessCommandLine) by SHA256, FileName, FolderPath;
let NewExec = RecentExec | join kind=leftanti BaselineExec on SHA256, FileName | extend Kind = "sshd/ssh exec";
let BaselineLoad = DeviceImageLoadEvents
    | where Timestamp between (ago(Lookback) .. ago(Recent))
    | where FileName == "pam_unix.so"
    | summarize by SHA256, FileName;
let RecentLoad = DeviceImageLoadEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(Recent)
    | where FileName == "pam_unix.so"
    | summarize FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), HostCount = dcount(DeviceId), AnyHost = any(DeviceName), AnyCmd = "" by SHA256, FileName, FolderPath;
let NewLoad = RecentLoad | join kind=leftanti BaselineLoad on SHA256, FileName | extend Kind = "pam_unix.so load";
union NewExec, NewLoad
| order by FirstSeen desc
let Lookback = 60d;
let Recent = 7d;
let AuthBinaries = dynamic(["sshd","ssh","scp","sftp","ssh-keygen","ssh-agent"]);
let Baseline = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(Lookback) .. ago(Recent))
    | where ActingProcessName in~ (AuthBinaries)
    | summarize by Hash = tostring(SHA256), ActingProcessName;
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(Recent)
| where ActingProcessName in~ (AuthBinaries)
| extend Hash = tostring(SHA256)
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on Hash, ActingProcessName
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), HostCount = dcount(DvcHostname), AnyHost = any(DvcHostname), AnyCmd = any(ActingProcessCommandLine) by Hash, ActingProcessName
| order by FirstSeen desc
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.executable.path:(/usr/sbin/sshd OR /usr/bin/sshd OR /usr/bin/ssh OR /usr/sbin/ssh OR /usr/bin/scp OR /usr/bin/sftp OR /usr/bin/ssh-keygen OR /usr/bin/ssh-agent) @process.executable.hash:*
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\/(usr\/sbin\/sshd|usr\/bin\/sshd|usr\/bin\/ssh|usr\/sbin\/ssh|usr\/bin\/scp|usr\/bin\/sftp|usr\/bin\/ssh-keygen|usr\/bin\/ssh-agent)$/i
| groupBy([SHA256HashData, ImageFileName], function={ min(_time, as=FirstSeen) | count(field=aid, distinct=true, as=HostCount) })
| join({#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\/(usr\/sbin\/sshd|usr\/bin\/sshd|usr\/bin\/ssh|usr\/sbin\/ssh|usr\/bin\/scp|usr\/bin\/sftp|usr\/bin\/ssh-keygen|usr\/bin\/ssh-agent)$/i _time<now()-7d | groupBy([SHA256HashData], function=count(as=BaselineCount))}, field=SHA256HashData, include=[BaselineCount], mode=left)
| BaselineCount=null
| sort(FirstSeen, order=desc)
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents

| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port

| order by conn_count desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer

status: experimental
description: |

    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.

            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'

        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'

Agentjacking Attack Tricks AI Coding Agents Into Running Malicious Code

The Hacker News
2026-06-12 11 use cases 5 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have described what they say is a new class of attack that can trick artificial intelligence (AI) coding agents into running arbitrary code on developer machines. Called Agentjacking by Tenet Security, the attack can be triggered by means of a fake error report crafted using Sentry, an open-source error-tracking and performance-monitoring platform. Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] AI coding agent (Claude Code / Cursor / Codex) spawning shell that fetch-and-executes remote payload
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Agentjacking C2/exfiltration to advisory-tracker.com (Tenet Sentry-MCP attack) · [LLM] AI coding agent descendant reading developer credentials / env (Agentjacking credential access) · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Agentjacking C2/exfiltration to advisory-tracker.com (Tenet Sentry-MCP attack) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the Tenet Security 'Agentjacking' exfiltration endpoint that receives developer environment variables, git credentials, repo URLs and tokens stolen by npm typosquat packages that a hijacked AI coding agent (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex) was tricked into installing via a forged Sentry issue. Both DNS resolution and TCP egress are pivoted because the npm-installed payload posts to https://advisory-tracker.com/api/v1/telemetry. Rationale: advisory-tracker.com and 52.206.47.180 are the Tenet-published exfiltration endpoint for the Agentjacking PoC, also enumerated in the PSPDFKit IOC repo for the related Sentry npm typosquat campaign. Cross-checked: Tenet's blog post and the PSPDFKit/sentry-npm-typosquat-2026-06-iocs GitHub repo both list the same domain + IP + /api/v1/telemetry path, so the IOC has independent corroboration beyond the THN article. Cross-checked against: • https://tenetsecurity.ai/blog/agentjacking-coding-agents-with-fake-sentry-errors/ • https://github.com/PSPDFKit/sentry-npm-typosquat-2026-06-iocs • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/agentjacking-attacks-hijack-ai/
ATT&CKT1041 T1071.001 T1567
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorised purple-team replay of the Tenet PoC from a research VM
  • Security-research sandbox detonating one of the IOC-listed npm packages
  • Threat-intel enrichment platform (VirusTotal/urlscan) auto-resolving advisory-tracker.com from a SOC analyst workstation
  • DNS-passive-replication sensor logging the domain without an actual host connecting
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\sandbox\", @"\detonation\", @"\threat-research\")) and not(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("vt-cli.exe","urlscan.exe","virustotal.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull DeviceProcessEvents for the same DeviceId in the 10 min before the connection, walk the process tree (claude.exe / cursor.exe / code.exe → node.exe → npm/npx → outbound), and confirm the developer was using an AI coding agent against Sentry. 2) Contain: isolate the host via Defender Live Response; immediately rotate every credential exposed in env on a developer box — git PAT, npm _authToken, AWS/GCP keys, .env secrets, Sentry DSN, any cloud-CLI session token. Quarantine the npm cache and node_modules under the suspect project. 3) Hunt: enumerate every host in the org that resolved advisory-tracker.com or hit 52.206.47.180 in the last 30 days; scan all developer repos for the typosquat package family in package-lock.json / yarn.lock; audit Sentry org membership against affected developers to find the injected issue ID.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "advisory-tracker.com" or RemoteIP == "52.206.47.180"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
union
  (ImNetworkSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where DstHostname has "advisory-tracker.com" or DstIpAddr == "52.206.47.180"
    | extend Indicator = coalesce(DstHostname, DstIpAddr)
    | project TimeGenerated, Source="ImNetworkSession", Host=DvcHostname, User=SrcUsername, Indicator, Url),
  (ImDnsActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where DnsQuery has "advisory-tracker.com"
    | project TimeGenerated, Source="ImDnsActivity", Host=SrcHostname, User=SrcUsername, Indicator=DnsQuery, Url=DnsQuery),
  (DnsEvents
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where Name has "advisory-tracker.com"
    | project TimeGenerated, Source="DnsEvents", Host=Computer, User=tostring(""), Indicator=Name, Url=Name)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Agentjacking exfiltration domain advisory-tracker.com resolved

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
