CVE-2026-48039 PoC artifact execution (docker image meta-ads-mcp-vuln001, FAKE_TOKEN_FOR_POC_DEMO) AIExploitation High
Detects known public-PoC artifacts for CVE-2026-48039: the `meta-ads-mcp-vuln001` Docker image referenced in the advisory PoC, the literal `FAKE_TOKEN_FOR_POC_DEMO_123456789` placeholder token shipped in the PoC environment, and execution of `poc.py` invoking the /mcp endpoint. High-confidence signal of either red-team testing or naive attacker tooling that hasn't customised the PoC. Rationale: Article PoC section names the exact strings: docker image `meta-ads-mcp-vuln001`, environment variable value `FAKE_TOKEN_FOR_POC_DEMO_123456789`, and the script name `poc.py`. These are PoC-specific literals that any operator copy-pasting the advisory will trigger — extremely low FP outside intentional security testing.
ATT&CKT1610 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized red-team or purple-team exercise reproducing the advisory PoC
  • Internal security researchers validating the patch
  • Vulnerability-management tool that runs the PoC for verification
  • Sandbox detonation environments analysing public exploit code
  • Documentation copies of the advisory committed to internal wiki / git that get scanned by EDR script-content collectors
Suppression filter
| where AccountName !in (dynamic(["<authorized-redteam-account>","<vm-validation-svc>"])) and DeviceName !in (dynamic(["<sandbox-host-1>","<security-lab-1>"]))
Response runbook
1. Triage: Identify the source — is this an authorized red-team exercise (check change-management / RoE records) or an unsanctioned execution? Pull the parent process tree to determine if it was launched interactively or via remote execution. 2. Contain: If unsanctioned, isolate the host, terminate the docker/podman container, kill the Python process, and capture container/process memory for forensics. Block egress from the host pending review. 3. Hunt: From the same source IP / user account, search for UC1 hits (POST /mcp from this host's IP), UC2 hits (graph.facebook.com URLs with access_token=) in the prior 30 days, and any other hosts in the estate that received connections from this source — the PoC may have been used to scan internal MCP servers.

    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Source="Process", FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, SHA256),

    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, Source="File", FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, SHA256)
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate

| extend Cmd = coalesce(TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessCommandLine)

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] FireAnt Metakit update process spawning script/LOLBin child (supply-chain payload exec)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — OceanLotus: From external espionage to domestic targeting
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] SPECTRALVIPER sample hash sighting (file/process/module load) · [LLM] SPECTRALVIPER selective second-stage payload drop post-FireAnt update · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] OceanLotus SPECTRALVIPER C&C infrastructure callback (dated IOC set) · [LLM] OceanLotus Denis/SOUNDBITE DNS tunneling — high-entropy subdomains + TXT abuse · [LLM] OceanLotus PHOREAL ICMP covert C&C — sustained outbound ICMP with non-standard payloads · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains · DNS tunneling / TXT-heavy domain queries
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
OceanLotus SPECTRALVIPER C&C infrastructure callback (dated IOC set) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound connections to the specific SPECTRALVIPER C&C IPs and domains documented in the ESET 2024-2026 campaigns. Each IP/domain pair is dated in the article's IOC table, so first-seen dates can be cross-referenced to suspected first-compromise time. Rationale: Uses the dated C&C table (gatewayrvcenter.com→139.180.128.42 first-seen 2025-09-20, coachcybersecurity.com→139.99.33.239 2024-07-08, mxprodesign.com→166.88.77.186 2024-07-12, power-sync-services.com→103.119.47.104 2024-07-06) plus financemachinelearning.com (article body), and the article's IOC IP block. Cross-checked against MITRE G0050/APT32 page and Elastic Security Labs 2023 SPECTRALVIPER write-up which lists overlapping OceanLotus infrastructure conventions. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0050/ • https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/elastic-charms-spectralviper
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004 T1583.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel research VMs visiting known-bad domains during analysis
  • Sinkhole providers (CIRCL, Spamhaus) that have absorbed any of these domains
  • Generic VPS reuse — the IPs are on shared hosters (Vultr/OVH/Linode); a benign tenant could rotate onto an IP after OceanLotus moves off
  • Security tool scheduled IOC validation tasks pinging the indicators
  • Reverse DNS/PTR lookups by infrastructure monitoring tools
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msedge.exe","chrome.exe","firefox.exe","iexplore.exe") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("--type=utility","--headless") | where AccountName !endswith "$" and AccountName !in~ ("threatintel","soc-research")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the InitiatingProcessFileName, SHA256, command line and parent for the hitting connection — if it's a browser/legitimate tool the analyst may be researching; check that the user account isn't a known threat-intel researcher. Pivot on DeviceId across the last 90d to find prior connections to the broader OceanLotus IOC set. 2) Contain: isolate the device via Defender Live Response, block the IP/domain at perimeter and EDR network containment, force-rotate AAD tokens for the AccountName. 3) Hunt: search DeviceProcessEvents/DeviceFileEvents for the SPECTRALVIPER SHA1s on the same device, sweep your fleet for any of the 6 domains/8 IPs across the full retention window, and check if the host runs FireAnt Metakit (likely first-stage if so).

SPECTRALVIPER sample hash sighting (file/process/module load) AIInstallation High
Matches the 20 SHA1s ESET attributes to SPECTRALVIPER samples observed in the FireAnt supply-chain and infrastructure-corporation campaigns. Any sighting in execution, file write, or DLL load telemetry is treated as confirmed OceanLotus presence. Rationale: Direct match against the 20 SHA1 hashes in the article's IOC block. Three telemetry views — process create, file write, image load — catch the binary regardless of whether it executes standalone, is dropped to disk, or is side-loaded as a DLL (OceanLotus's known DLL side-load TTP per MITRE G0050). Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0050/ • https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/elastic-charms-spectralviper
ATT&CKT1059 T1574.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sandboxing/EDR/AV tools writing the sample for analysis on a research VM
  • VirusTotal/Hybrid-Analysis intel ingestion writing samples to disk in a research path
  • Honeypot detonation infrastructure
  • Backup of a previously infected machine being restored containing dormant copies of the binary
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath !contains "\\Quarantine\\" and FolderPath !contains "\\Sandbox\\" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","MpCmdRun.exe","SenseIR.exe","hybrid-analysis-collector.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree around the SHA1 sighting — Defender DeviceProcessEvents with ProcessId/ProcessCreationTime/InitiatingProcess* to identify how the binary got onto the host (FireAnt update? signed installer DLL side-load? scheduled task?). 2) Contain: EDR-isolate the host, quarantine the file by hash org-wide via Defender file blocking, force credential rotation for the AccountName and all logged-on users in the previous 30d (DeviceLogonEvents). 3) Hunt: sweep DeviceNetworkEvents on the same DeviceId for the C&C IPs/domains in UC1, check DeviceProcessEvents/DeviceFileEvents for FireAnt Metakit presence, and run UC4/UC5 against the same host to identify Denis (DNS) or PHOREAL (ICMP) auxiliary implants.

FireAnt Metakit update process spawning script/LOLBin child (supply-chain payload exec) AIDelivery Medium
FireAnt Metakit's updater was compromised between Oct 2025 and Mar 2026 and pushed SPECTRALVIPER to selected investors. Hunts the post-update execution chain: the FireAnt updater spawning script engines / LOLBins / unsigned binaries from a writable user directory — the exact shape of a poisoned-updater payload drop. Rationale: Anchored on the FireAnt Metakit campaign (article: 'compromised the update server of FireAnt Metakit ... replaced legitimate software updates with a malicious payload that ultimately deployed SPECTRALVIPER', Oct 2025-Mar 2026). The detection key is the parent-image string match on FireAnt/Metakit because the legitimate updater should never spawn script engines or LOLBins. We treat it as hunting because we have no leaked binary name from the article — pattern match on the product name is the best available pivot. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/oceanlotus-external-espionage-domestic-targeting/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.001 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • FireAnt updater calling msiexec for a legitimate signed MSI patch
  • FireAnt support utility spawning cmd to gather diagnostic info during a user-initiated 'send logs' action
  • Group Policy / SCCM removing a FireAnt installation by invoking msiexec under the FireAnt installer path
  • Endpoint security agent re-parented onto the FireAnt process tree mid-scan
Suppression filter
| where ChildCmd !has "--diagnostic" and ChildCmd !has "\\logs\\" and not (Child =~ "msiexec.exe" and ChildCmd has "/quiet" and ChildCmd has "FireAnt")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the SHA256 of both parent (FireAnt binary) and child against VirusTotal and the SPECTRALVIPER SHA1 list from UC2 — the article notes the malicious update was distributed Oct 2025 to Mar 2026, so any hit in that window is high-priority. Identify the user's role (stock investor / finance), aligning with the campaign's victim profile. 2) Contain: isolate the device, block the FireAnt parent SHA256 if confirmed malicious, file an abuse notification with FireAnt (article notes ESET tried and 'received no response' — escalate via national CERT VNCERT). 3) Hunt: pivot to UC1 (C&C IPs/domains) and UC2 (sample SHA1s) on the same host, sweep all hosts running FireAnt Metakit (DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory where SoftwareName has "FireAnt") for the same parent SHA256 across Oct 2025-Mar 2026.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(180d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has "fireant" 
   or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("FireAnt","Metakit","fireant")
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("FireAnt","Metakit","fireantapp")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","msiexec.exe")
   or (FolderPath has_any ("\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\","\\AppData\\Roaming\\","\\ProgramData\\","\\Users\\Public\\") and ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName !has "FireAnt")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          Parent = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          ParentFolder = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          Child = FileName,
          ChildFolder = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256, SHA1
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(180d)
| where ParentProcessName has "fireant" or ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("FireAnt","Metakit")
| where ActingProcessName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","msiexec.exe")
   or (ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\","\\AppData\\Roaming\\","\\ProgramData\\","\\Users\\Public\\") and ActingProcessFileCompany !has "FireAnt")
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine,
          SHA1, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

      - '\regsvr32.exe'
      - '\bitsadmin.exe'
      - '\certutil.exe'
      - '\curl.exe'
      - '\wget.exe'
      - '\msiexec.exe'
  condition: parent_fireant and child_suspicious
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\\FireAnt* OR *\\fireant* OR *\\Metakit* OR *\\metakit*) @Image:(*\\powershell.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe OR *\\pwsh.exe OR *\\cmd.exe OR *\\CMD.exe OR *\\mshta.exe OR *\\MSHTA.exe OR *\\wscript.exe OR *\\cscript.exe OR *\\rundll32.exe OR *\\RunDLL32.exe OR *\\regsvr32.exe OR *\\bitsadmin.exe OR *\\certutil.exe OR *\\curl.exe OR *\\wget.exe OR *\\msiexec.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/fireant|metakit/i
| ImageFileName=/(powershell|pwsh|cmd|mshta|wscript|cscript|rundll32|regsvr32|bitsadmin|certutil|curl|wget|msiexec)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=[count(), min(@timestamp, as=first_seen)])
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as first_seen max(_time) as last_seen values(Processes.process) as cmd values(Processes.process_path) as path values(Processes.parent_process) as parent_cmd values(Processes.user) as user from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name="*fireant*" OR Processes.parent_process_path="*FireAnt*" OR Processes.parent_process_path="*Metakit*" OR Processes.parent_process="*fireant*update*") AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","msiexec.exe") by Processes.dest Processes.process_name Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

OceanLotus Denis/SOUNDBITE DNS tunneling — high-entropy subdomains + TXT abuse AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the signature of OceanLotus's Denis (aka SOUNDBITE) backdoor, which the article names as implementing DNS tunneling for C&C. Surfaces hosts emitting many distinct high-entropy subdomains under a single parent, or sustained TXT-record queries — both characteristic of DNS-tunneled command/exfiltration. Rationale: Article explicitly names Denis/SOUNDBITE as an OceanLotus tool 'implementing DNS tunneling for C&C communications'. We hunt the canonical DNS-tunnel shape: many unique high-entropy subdomains under a single parent within a short window, plus TXT-record abuse. Allowlist baseline CDN/cloud parents to keep noise manageable. Threshold (30 distinct subs, avg length 25) is from the BluRaven baseline reference; tune per environment. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0050/ • https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0157/
ATT&CKT1071.004 T1048.003
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Telemetry agents (Datadog, Splunk UF, New Relic) that use long unique session-id subdomains for cache-busting
  • Cisco Umbrella / Zscaler reverse-DNS health checks
  • Anti-spam DKIM/DMARC lookups (DKIM selectors look like high-entropy subdomains)
  • Akamai/CloudFront/Fastly CDNs that mint per-asset hostnames
  • DNS-based ad-blocker or AV update channels (e.g., Sophos LiveProtection's hash queries)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("datadog-agent.exe","splunk-uf.exe","NewRelic.Server.exe","umbrella-deployment.exe","AmpDaemon.exe") and Parent !endswith ".akamaiedge.net" and Parent !endswith ".datadoghq.com"
Response runbook
1) Triage: enumerate the InitiatingProcessFileName driving the queries — legitimate svchost.exe doing DKIM lookups vs. an unsigned binary doing TXT queries are night-and-day. Pivot the same DeviceId to UC1 to see whether it also hit known SPECTRALVIPER C&C. 2) Contain: if the process is unsigned or matches UC2 hash list, EDR-isolate; block the parent domain at recursive resolver. 3) Hunt: pull DeviceProcessEvents for the InitiatingProcessId to identify the binary path, capture the binary for malware analysis, and search the fleet for the same parent domain (UC1-style IOC sweep) since Denis/SOUNDBITE C&C domains are typically reused.
let WindowSize = 1h;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "DnsQueryResponse"
| where isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| extend Labels = split(RemoteUrl, ".")
| extend LabelCount = array_length(Labels)
| where LabelCount >= 3
| extend Sub = tostring(Labels[0])
| extend Parent = strcat(tostring(Labels[LabelCount-2]), ".", tostring(Labels[LabelCount-1]))
| extend SubLen = strlen(Sub)
| where Parent !in ("in-addr.arpa","ip6.arpa","google.com","microsoft.com","windows.com","office.com","akamaiedge.net","cloudfront.net","amazonaws.com")
| summarize TotalQueries = count(),
            DistinctSubs = dcount(Sub),
            AvgSubLen    = avg(SubLen),
            MaxSubLen    = max(SubLen),
            SampleQueries = make_set(RemoteUrl, 5)
           by DeviceId, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, Parent, bin(Timestamp, WindowSize)
| where DistinctSubs >= 30 and AvgSubLen >= 25
| order by DistinctSubs desc
let WindowSize = 1h;
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where isnotempty(DnsQuery)
| extend Labels = split(DnsQuery, ".")
| extend LabelCount = array_length(Labels)
| where LabelCount >= 3
| extend Sub = tostring(Labels[0])
| extend Parent = strcat(tostring(Labels[LabelCount-2]), ".", tostring(Labels[LabelCount-1]))
| extend SubLen = strlen(Sub)
| where Parent !in ("in-addr.arpa","ip6.arpa","google.com","microsoft.com","windows.com","office.com","akamaiedge.net","cloudfront.net","amazonaws.com")
| summarize TotalQueries = count(),
            DistinctSubs = dcount(Sub),
            AvgSubLen    = avg(SubLen),
            MaxSubLen    = max(SubLen),
            TxtCount     = countif(DnsQueryTypeName =~ "TXT"),
            SampleQueries = make_set(DnsQuery, 5)
           by SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, Parent, bin(TimeGenerated, WindowSize)
| where (DistinctSubs >= 30 and AvgSubLen >= 25) or TxtCount >= 50
| order by DistinctSubs desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:22 @QueryName:* -@QueryName:(*.in-addr.arpa OR *.ip6.arpa OR *.windows.com OR *.microsoft.com OR *.office.com OR *.google.com OR *.akamaiedge.net OR *.cloudfront.net OR *.amazonaws.com)
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest
| DomainName!=/\.(in-addr\.arpa|ip6\.arpa|windows\.com|microsoft\.com|office\.com|google\.com|akamaiedge\.net|cloudfront\.net|amazonaws\.com)$/i
| firstLabel := splitString(field=DomainName, by="\\.", index=0)
| firstLabelLen := length(firstLabel)
| timeBucket(span=1h)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, _bucket], function=[count(as=total), count(field=firstLabel, distinct=true, as=distinctSubs), avg(firstLabelLen, as=avgSubLen)])
| distinctSubs >= 30
| avgSubLen >= 25
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count dc(DNS.query) as unique_queries values(DNS.record_type) as record_types from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS where DNS.query="*.*" by DNS.src DNS.query bin(_time, 1h) | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)` | rex field=query "^(?<sub>[^\.]+)\.(?<parent>.+)$" | eval sub_len=len(sub) | stats sum(count) as total_qs dc(query) as distinct_subs avg(sub_len) as avg_sub_len max(sub_len) as max_sub_len values(record_types) as record_types by src parent _time | where distinct_subs >= 30 AND avg_sub_len >= 25 AND parent!="in-addr.arpa" AND parent!="ip6.arpa"
| tstats summariesonly=false count dc(DNS.query) as unique_queries values(DNS.record_type) as record_types from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS where DNS.query="*.*" by DNS.src DNS.query bin(_time, 1h) | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)` | rex field=query "^(?<sub>[^\.]+)\.(?<parent>.+)$" | eval sub_len=len(sub) | stats sum(count) as total_qs dc(query) as distinct_subs avg(sub_len) as avg_sub_len max(sub_len) as max_sub_len values(record_types) as record_types by src parent _time | where distinct_subs >= 30 AND avg_sub_len >= 25 AND parent!="in-addr.arpa" AND parent!="ip6.arpa"
OceanLotus PHOREAL ICMP covert C&C — sustained outbound ICMP with non-standard payloads AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts OceanLotus's PHOREAL backdoor, which the article identifies as leveraging the ICMP protocol for C&C. Surfaces sustained outbound ICMP from endpoints to public IPs, especially correlated with non-ICMP-emitting processes (PHOREAL uses raw sockets to embed C&C in ping payloads). Rationale: Article explicitly names PHOREAL as an OceanLotus backdoor 'leveraging the ICMP protocol for C&C communications'. Detection logic: outbound ICMP from a non-utility process to a public IP, sustained over 30 minutes with 30+ events — way outside normal Windows ICMP profile (legitimate ICMP is dominated by ping.exe one-shots and network monitoring tools). Allowlists exclude ping/tracert/pathping which legitimately use ICMP. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0050/ • https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0158/
ATT&CKT1071 T1095
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Network monitoring tools (PRTG, SolarWinds, Nagios) installed on Windows endpoints doing perimeter health pings
  • Custom in-house monitoring scripts that ping external SLAs/uptime endpoints from workstations
  • Sophos/Cisco AnyConnect doing peer-tunnel ICMP keepalives that show as public destinations pre-tunnel
  • Smokeping or RIPE Atlas probes installed for network research
  • Misconfigured load balancer / VPN client doing ICMP path MTU discovery
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("prtg probe.exe","PRTGProbe.exe","SolarWinds.Pingdom.exe","WhatsUp Gold.exe","Nagios.exe","smokeping.exe","vpnagent.exe","AnyConnect.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcessFileName/SHA256 — legitimate monitoring tools (PRTG agent, SolarWinds) are obvious; anything unsigned/unknown writing raw ICMP is high-priority. Pivot to UC1/UC2 on the same DeviceId to check for known OceanLotus IOCs. 2) Contain: if the process is unknown, EDR-isolate the host and block ICMP egress from the workstation VLAN at the firewall (most workstations don't need outbound ICMP). 3) Hunt: capture the binary for malware analysis, sweep the fleet for the same InitiatingProcessSHA256, and pull a pcap on the next observed ICMP burst — PHOREAL embeds C&C in the ping payload which a packet capture will surface as non-zero, non-standard echo data.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Protocol =~ "Icmp"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("system","")
   and InitiatingProcessFileName !endswith "ping.exe"
   and InitiatingProcessFileName !endswith "tracert.exe"
   and InitiatingProcessFileName !endswith "pathping.exe"
| summarize IcmpEvents = count(),
            DistinctRemoteIPs = dcount(RemoteIP),
            FirstSeen = min(Timestamp),
            LastSeen  = max(Timestamp),
            DurationMin = datetime_diff('minute', max(Timestamp), min(Timestamp)),
            RemoteIPs = make_set(RemoteIP, 10)
           by DeviceId, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| where IcmpEvents >= 30 and DurationMin >= 30
| order by IcmpEvents desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where NetworkProtocol =~ "ICMP" or NetworkProtocol == "1"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false and DstIpAddr !startswith "169.254." and DstIpAddr !startswith "127."
| summarize IcmpEvents = count(),
            DistinctRemoteIPs = dcount(DstIpAddr),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen  = max(TimeGenerated),
            DurationMin = datetime_diff('minute', max(TimeGenerated), min(TimeGenerated)),
            RemoteIPs = make_set(DstIpAddr, 10)
           by SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, EventProduct
| where IcmpEvents >= 30 and DurationMin >= 30
| order by IcmpEvents desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @Protocol:icmp -@Image:(*\\ping.exe OR *\\PING.EXE OR *\\tracert.exe OR *\\TRACERT.EXE OR *\\pathping.exe)
(#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 OR #event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP6) Protocol=1
| NOT cidr("10.0.0.0/8", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| NOT cidr("172.16.0.0/12", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| NOT cidr("192.168.0.0/16", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| NOT ContextImageFileName=/\\(ping|tracert|pathping)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemoteAddressIP4], function=[count(as=icmp_pkts), min(@timestamp, as=first_seen), max(@timestamp, as=last_seen)])
| icmp_pkts >= 30
# log group: /aws/vpc/flowlogs
fields @timestamp, srcAddr, dstAddr, protocol, packets, bytes, action
| filter protocol = 1 and action = "ACCEPT"
| filter dstAddr not like /^10\./ and dstAddr not like /^192\.168\./ and dstAddr not like /^172\.(1[6-9]|2[0-9]|3[01])\./
| stats sum(packets) as icmp_packets, count_distinct(dstAddr) as distinct_dsts, min(@timestamp) as first_seen, max(@timestamp) as last_seen by srcAddr, dstAddr
| filter icmp_packets >= 30
| sort icmp_packets desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.transport="icmp" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal" by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.app _time span=10m | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | stats sum(count) as icmp_pkts dc(dest) as distinct_dests min(_time) as first_seen max(_time) as last_seen values(app) as process by src dest | where icmp_pkts >= 30
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.transport="icmp" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal" by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.app _time span=10m | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | stats sum(count) as icmp_pkts dc(dest) as distinct_dests min(_time) as first_seen max(_time) as last_seen values(app) as process by src dest | where icmp_pkts >= 30
SPECTRALVIPER selective second-stage payload drop post-FireAnt update AIInstallation Medium
Article notes that despite broad FireAnt user exposure, 'only a few individuals who ultimately received SPECTRALVIPER' — implying a victim-selection check followed by a second-stage write. Hunts file drops to user-writable persistence paths by FireAnt-spawned processes, capturing the moment selective targeting promotes from staged dropper to active backdoor. Rationale: Article body: 'only a few individuals who ultimately received SPECTRALVIPER, indicating selective targeting' — the dropper checks the victim, then writes the payload. We detect the moment of stage-2 commitment: the FireAnt updater (parent string match on FireAnt/Metakit) writing an executable/script to a writable path, OR setting a Run-key value. Unioning file-drop + autorun-write captures both deployment paths a custom backdoor with 'orchestration capabilities' (article) would use. Cross-checked against MITRE G0050 which lists T1547.001 as a known OceanLotus persistence technique. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0050/ • https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/elastic-charms-spectralviper
ATT&CKT1105 T1547.001 T1574.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • FireAnt legitimate updater writing a real signed patch DLL/EXE to its own install path (allowlist by signature)
  • FireAnt logging component writing .log-renamed-to-.txt files (extension allowlist excludes .log)
  • User installing a FireAnt plugin/extension that legitimately drops to AppData
  • FireAnt crash dump writer creating .dmp files (extension allowlist excludes .dmp)
  • Enterprise MDM repackaging FireAnt and dropping config files
Suppression filter
| where DroppedFile !endswith ".log" and DroppedFile !endswith ".dmp" and DroppedFile !endswith ".tmp" and DroppedPath !contains "\\FireAnt\\Updates\\Verified\\" and not (DroppedSHA256 in (dynamic([])) )
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the SHA256 of both the parent (FireAnt binary) and the dropped file. If the dropped SHA matches the UC2 SPECTRALVIPER hash list — confirmed incident, escalate to IR immediately. Otherwise, submit dropped file to detonation. Note the AccountName: article suggests stock investors and infrastructure/transport corp employees are the target profile. 2) Contain: EDR-isolate the host, quarantine the dropped file by SHA256 across the fleet, block the parent FireAnt binary hash if confirmed malicious. 3) Hunt: from the same DeviceId, run UC1 (C&C beacons) and UC4/UC5 (Denis DNS / PHOREAL ICMP), sweep DeviceFileEvents fleet-wide for the dropped SHA256, and pull DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory for the FireAnt version on impacted hosts to identify the malicious update package version.
let SuspiciousExtensions = dynamic([".exe",".dll",".bat",".ps1",".vbs",".js",".hta",".lnk",".scr"]);
let WritablePaths = dynamic(["\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\","\\AppData\\Local\\","\\AppData\\Roaming\\","\\ProgramData\\","\\Users\\Public\\","\\Windows\\Temp\\"]);
let FireAntFileWrites = DeviceFileEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(180d)
  | where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified")
  | where InitiatingProcessFileName has "fireant"
     or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("FireAnt","Metakit")
  | where FolderPath has_any (WritablePaths)
  | extend Ext = tolower(strcat(".", tostring(split(FileName, ".")[-1])))
  | where Ext in (SuspiciousExtensions)
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName,
            DroppedFile = FileName, DroppedPath = FolderPath, DroppedSHA1 = SHA1, DroppedSHA256 = SHA256,
            Parent = InitiatingProcessFileName, ParentPath = InitiatingProcessFolderPath, ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, DeviceId;
let FireAntRunKey = DeviceRegistryEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(180d)
  | where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated")
  | where RegistryKey has_any ("\\CurrentVersion\\Run","\\CurrentVersion\\RunOnce","\\Image File Execution Options\\","\\AppInit_DLLs")
  | where InitiatingProcessFileName has "fireant"
     or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("FireAnt","Metakit")
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName,
            RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData,
            Parent = InitiatingProcessFileName, ParentPath = InitiatingProcessFolderPath, ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, DeviceId;
union FireAntFileWrites, FireAntRunKey
| order by Timestamp desc
let SuspiciousExtensions = dynamic([".exe",".dll",".bat",".ps1",".vbs",".js",".hta",".lnk",".scr"]);
let WritablePaths = dynamic(["\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\","\\AppData\\Local\\","\\AppData\\Roaming\\","\\ProgramData\\","\\Users\\Public\\","\\Windows\\Temp\\"]);
let FireAntWrites = ImFileEvent
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(180d)
  | where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified")
  | where ActingProcessName has "fireant" or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("FireAnt","Metakit")
  | where TargetFilePath has_any (WritablePaths)
  | extend Ext = tolower(TargetFileExtension)
  | where strcat(".", Ext) in (SuspiciousExtensions)
  | project TimeGenerated, Host=DvcHostname, User=ActorUsername,
            DroppedFile=TargetFileName, DroppedPath=TargetFilePath, DroppedSHA1=TargetFileSHA1, DroppedSHA256=TargetFileSHA256,
            Parent=ActingProcessName, ParentCmd=ActingProcessCommandLine;
let FireAntRunKey = ImRegistryEvent
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(180d)
  | where EventType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated")
  | where RegistryKey has_any ("\\CurrentVersion\\Run","\\CurrentVersion\\RunOnce","\\Image File Execution Options\\","\\AppInit_DLLs")
  | where ActingProcessName has "fireant" or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("FireAnt","Metakit")
  | project TimeGenerated, Host=DvcHostname, User=ActorUsername,
            DroppedFile=RegistryValue, DroppedPath=RegistryKey, DroppedSHA1="", DroppedSHA256="",
            Parent=ActingProcessName, ParentCmd=ActingProcessCommandLine;
union FireAntWrites, FireAntRunKey
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: FireAnt Updater Writing Executable Payload or Run-Key (SPECTRALVIPER Stage 2)
id: a3f7d9c1-8b4e-4d2f-9f0e-3c2d1b4e5a99
description: Detects the second-stage payload drop from OceanLotus FireAnt Metakit supply-chain compromise (Oct 2025-Mar 2026) — the FireAnt updater writing PE/script files to user-writable persistence paths or setting Run-key autostarts. Article notes only a subset of FireAnt users received SPECTRALVIPER, suggesting selective second-stage delivery.
references:
  - https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/oceanlotus-external-espionage-domestic-targeting/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/19
tags:
  - attack.execution
  - attack.t1105
  - attack.persistence
  - attack.t1547.001
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_parent:
    Image|contains:
      - '\FireAnt'
      - '\fireant'
      - '\Metakit'
  selection_path:
    TargetFilename|contains:
      - '\AppData\Local\Temp\'
      - '\AppData\Local\'
      - '\AppData\Roaming\'
      - '\ProgramData\'
      - '\Users\Public\'
      - '\Windows\Temp\'
  selection_ext:
    TargetFilename|endswith:
      - '.exe'
      - '.dll'
      - '.bat'
      - '.ps1'
      - '.vbs'
      - '.js'
      - '.hta'
      - '.lnk'
      - '.scr'
  condition: all of selection_*
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @Image:(*\\FireAnt* OR *\\fireant* OR *\\Metakit* OR *\\metakit*) @TargetFilename:(*\\AppData\\* OR *\\ProgramData\\* OR *\\Users\\Public\\* OR *\\Windows\\Temp\\*) @TargetFilename:(*.exe OR *.dll OR *.bat OR *.ps1 OR *.vbs OR *.js OR *.hta OR *.lnk OR *.scr)
(#event_simpleName=FileWritten OR #event_simpleName=AsepValueUpdate) ContextImageFileName=/fireant|metakit/i
| (TargetFileName=/\\(AppData|ProgramData|Users\\Public|Windows\\Temp)\\/i AND TargetFileName=/\.(exe|dll|bat|ps1|vbs|js|hta|lnk|scr)$/i) OR RegObjectName=/\\(CurrentVersion\\Run|CurrentVersion\\RunOnce|Image File Execution Options|AppInit_DLLs)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName, RegObjectName, RegStringValue], function=[count(), min(@timestamp, as=first_seen)])
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as first_seen values(Filesystem.file_name) as file_name values(Filesystem.file_path) as file_path values(Filesystem.process_name) as process_name from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.process_name="*fireant*" OR Filesystem.process_path="*FireAnt*" OR Filesystem.process_path="*Metakit*") AND Filesystem.file_name IN ("*.exe","*.dll","*.bat","*.ps1","*.vbs","*.js","*.hta") AND (Filesystem.file_path="*\\AppData\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\ProgramData\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Users\\Public\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Temp\\*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as first_seen values(Filesystem.file_name) as file_name values(Filesystem.file_path) as file_path values(Filesystem.process_name) as process_name from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.process_name="*fireant*" OR Filesystem.process_path="*FireAnt*" OR Filesystem.process_path="*Metakit*") AND Filesystem.file_name IN ("*.exe","*.dll","*.bat","*.ps1","*.vbs","*.js","*.hta") AND (Filesystem.file_path="*\\AppData\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\ProgramData\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Users\\Public\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Temp\\*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("139.162.11.152", "142.91.98.77", "139.180.128.42", "139.99.33.239", "166.88.77.186", "103.119.47.104", "38.60.245.37", "194.68.26.241") or RemoteUrl has_any ("financemachinelearning.com", "gatewayrvcenter.com", "coachcybersecurity.com", "mxprodesign.com", "power-sync-services.com", "leadingfilipinoteams.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
let BadIPs     = dynamic(["139.162.11.152", "142.91.98.77", "139.180.128.42", "139.99.33.239", "166.88.77.186", "103.119.47.104", "38.60.245.37", "194.68.26.241"]);
let BadDomains = dynamic(["financemachinelearning.com", "gatewayrvcenter.com", "coachcybersecurity.com", "mxprodesign.com", "power-sync-services.com", "leadingfilipinoteams.com"]);
ImNetworkSession

title: Outbound Connection to Article-Named IP / Domain
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0f
status: experimental
description: |

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

    where All_Traffic.dest IN ("139.162.11.152", "142.91.98.77", "139.180.128.42", "139.99.33.239", "166.88.77.186", "103.119.47.104", "38.60.245.37", "194.68.26.241")
    by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest, All_Traffic.dest_port
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`

    [| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Web
        where Web.dest IN ("financemachinelearning.com", "gatewayrvcenter.com", "coachcybersecurity.com", "mxprodesign.com", "power-sync-services.com", "leadingfilipinoteams.com")
        by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.url, Web.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`]
| append
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS
        where DNS.query IN ("financemachinelearning.com", "gatewayrvcenter.com", "coachcybersecurity.com", "mxprodesign.com", "power-sync-services.com", "leadingfilipinoteams.com")
        by DNS.src, DNS.query, DNS.answer
     | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`]
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.dest IN ("139.162.11.152", "142.91.98.77", "139.180.128.42", "139.99.33.239", "166.88.77.186", "103.119.47.104", "38.60.245.37", "194.68.26.241")
    by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest, All_Traffic.dest_port
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| append
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web
        where Web.dest IN ("financemachinelearning.com", "gatewayrvcenter.com", "coachcybersecurity.com", "mxprodesign.com", "power-sync-services.com", "leadingfilipinoteams.com")
        by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.url, Web.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`]
| append
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS
        where DNS.query IN ("financemachinelearning.com", "gatewayrvcenter.com", "coachcybersecurity.com", "mxprodesign.com", "power-sync-services.com", "leadingfilipinoteams.com")
        by DNS.src, DNS.query, DNS.answer
     | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`]
DNS tunneling / TXT-heavy domain queries Command & Control Medium
Long subdomain labels + frequent queries to a single 2LD = DNS C2/exfil.
ATT&CKT1071.004 T1048.003
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemotePort == 53 and isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| extend qlen = strlen(RemoteUrl)
| where qlen > 50
| extend SecondLevelDomain = extract(@"([\w-]+\.[a-zA-Z]{2,})$", 1, RemoteUrl)
| summarize qcount = count(), uniqueSubs = dcount(RemoteUrl), maxLabel = max(qlen)
    by DeviceName, SecondLevelDomain
| where qcount > 100 and uniqueSubs > 20
| order by qcount desc
// ASIM ImDnsActivity normalises Windows DNS, Sysmon EID 22, Linux dnsmasq, etc.
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where DnsQueryTypeName == "TXT"
| summarize Queries = count(), DistinctNames = dcount(DnsQuery)
            by SrcIpAddr, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where Queries > 200    // tune to TXT-query baseline for environment
| order by Queries desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS
    where DNS.message_type="QUERY"
    by DNS.src, DNS.query
| `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`
| eval qlen=len(query)
| where qlen > 50
| rex field=query "(?<second_level_domain>[\w-]+\.[\w-]+)$"
| stats sum(count) AS qcount, dc(query) AS unique_subs, max(qlen) AS max_label
    by src, second_level_domain
| where qcount > 100 AND unique_subs > 20
| sort - qcount
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS
    where DNS.message_type="QUERY"
    by DNS.src, DNS.query
| `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`
| eval qlen=len(query)
| where qlen > 50
| rex field=query "(?<second_level_domain>[\w-]+\.[\w-]+)$"
| stats sum(count) AS qcount, dc(query) AS unique_subs, max(qlen) AS max_label
    by src, second_level_domain
| where qcount > 100 AND unique_subs > 20
| sort - qcount
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |

    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:

author: Clankerusecase

        Image|endswith:
            - '\psexec.exe'

            - '\psexesvc.exe'
            - '\paexec.exe'
            - '\csexec.exe'
            - '\remcom.exe'

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("D511B77459673EC42163F19E300FF1D233B6C39F", "59A8553A4F8130F576AB234E0B220BE4D4DA0E98", "9CA1A5C7F79882DB913534C1E62B26BCDCB9F6DD", Ivanti Sentry (formerly known as MobileIron Sentry) contains an OS command injection vulnerability which could allow a remote unauthenticated user to achieve root-level remote code execution. Vulnerable Baileys npm package present on disk (CVE-2026-48063) AIWeaponization Medium
Surfaces hosts where the Baileys WhatsApp library is installed under node_modules so an analyst can pivot version vs. the CVE-2026-48063 fixed bounds (< 6.7.22 on v6, < 7.0.0-rc12 on v7). Pure asset-inventory pivot — combine with a follow-up read of package.json to extract version. Rationale: GHSA-qvv5-jq5g-4cgg explicitly names affected packages 'baileys' and '@whiskeysockets/baileys' with fixed versions 6.7.22 and 7.0.0-rc12. package.json under those node_modules subpaths is the unambiguous on-disk artifact. Cross-checked: https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qvv5-jq5g-4cgg, https://github.com/WhiskeySockets/Baileys (patch commit 3beb08e). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qvv5-jq5g-4cgg • https://github.com/WhiskeySockets/Baileys/commit/3beb08eecfcb4e65722e674034bd84fb11a9de35
ATT&CKT1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate WhatsApp bot/chat server already patched to >=6.7.22 or >=7.0.0-rc12 (true positive on inventory, false positive on alert — must read version from package.json)
  • Developer workstation with a checked-out copy of the Baileys source repository for contribution work
  • CI/CD build agent that transiently materialises the package during npm install before publishing the artifact
  • Test/sandbox VM intentionally running an old Baileys to reproduce the vuln
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("node.exe", "npm.exe", "yarn.exe", "pnpm.exe") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "install"
Response runbook
1. TRIAGE — for each hit, read the package.json `version` field; if >=6.7.22 (v6) or >=7.0.0-rc12 (v7) close as not-vulnerable. Identify the owning service (systemd unit, PM2 process, container) and business owner. 2. CONTAIN — if vulnerable and exposed to untrusted WhatsApp peers, request the team upgrade via `npm i baileys@latest` / `@whiskeysockets/baileys@latest` or apply the workaround (drop messages.upsert events with requestId field, set shouldSyncHistoryMessage: () => false). 3. HUNT — pivot to UC2 to find when the vulnerable version was installed and by whom; pivot to UC3/UC5 to check for in-the-wild exploitation against the host.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "package.json"
| where FolderPath endswith @"\node_modules\baileys" or FolderPath endswith @"\node_modules\@whiskeysockets\baileys"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Hits=count() by DeviceName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by LastSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "package.json"
| where TargetFilePath endswith @"\node_modules\baileys\package.json" or TargetFilePath endswith @"\node_modules\@whiskeysockets\baileys\package.json"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Hits=count() by DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName
| order by LastSeen desc

Baileys npm package install or upgrade activity AIDelivery Medium
Detects npm/yarn/pnpm/npx invocations installing or upgrading the Baileys WhatsApp library on managed hosts. Catches fresh introductions of the vulnerable code into dev/release pipelines and identifies who/when so the asset inventory in UC1 stays current. Rationale: Article explicitly names affected packages 'baileys' and '@whiskeysockets/baileys' and a versioned fix; detecting install/upgrade verbs gives temporal context (who introduced it, when) which is missing from a pure file-presence query. Cross-checked: https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qvv5-jq5g-4cgg. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qvv5-jq5g-4cgg
ATT&CKT1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Engineering team's intentional patch to 6.7.22 / 7.0.0-rc12 (good — UC should fire so SOC confirms patch landed)
  • CI pipeline running `npm ci` on every build, generating recurring hits per build agent
  • Developer running `npm update` to refresh transitive deps without intending to touch Baileys
  • Renovate/Dependabot bot account performing scheduled upgrade PR commits
  • Docker build stage running on container build hosts
Suppression filter
| where AccountName !endswith "$" and AccountName !in~ ("renovate-bot", "dependabot[bot]", "github-actions")
Response runbook
1. TRIAGE — read the full command line. Was it `npm install baileys@6.7.22` (good patch), `npm install baileys` (latest, ambiguous), or `npm install baileys@6.7.10` (introducing vuln)? Check user/account against approved engineering identities. 2. CONTAIN — if pinned to a vulnerable version on a non-build host, contact owner and request upgrade; if from an unknown account on a host that shouldn't run npm, isolate the host. 3. HUNT — within 24h before this event, look for the source of the command (CI job, shell session, IDE). After this event, run UC1 to confirm install completed and pivot to UC3/UC5 for any exploitation signs.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("npm.exe", "yarn.exe", "pnpm.exe", "npx.exe")
   or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm.exe", "yarn.exe", "pnpm.exe", "npx.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("baileys", "@whiskeysockets/baileys")
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("baileys", "@whiskeysockets/baileys")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("install", "add", "update", "upgrade")
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("install", "add", "update", "upgrade")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("npm.exe", "yarn.exe", "pnpm.exe", "npx.exe")
| where CommandLine has_any ("baileys", "@whiskeysockets/baileys")
| where CommandLine has_any ("install", "add", "update", "upgrade")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Baileys protocolMessage exploit signature: placeholderResendMessage + requestId AIExploitation High
Hunts for the post-exploitation artifact in Baileys application logs: a messages.upsert event carrying a requestId field together with handling of protocolMessage / placeholderResendMessage. This combination is the article's stated exploit chain for spoofing fake messages and history sync. Rationale: Article explicitly identifies the exploit primitive: 'malicious payload via the placeholderResendMessage' triggers a 'fake messages.upsert event' and the documented workaround is 'dropping messages.upsert events that contain a requestId field' — confirming requestId is the high-fidelity differentiator. Defender/Falcon queries are process-pivots only since EDR does not capture WebSocket app payloads; the real detection lives in the Node app log stream (Sentinel Syslog, Splunk index, Datadog). Cross-checked: https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qvv5-jq5g-4cgg. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qvv5-jq5g-4cgg • https://github.com/WhiskeySockets/Baileys/commit/3beb08eecfcb4e65722e674034bd84fb11a9de35
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.007
Data sourcesApplication logs (no CIM datamodel — raw Syslog/app)
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Verbose-debug logging that prints every messages.upsert payload, where benign upserts coincidentally co-mention protocolMessage in adjacent log lines within the same bucket
  • Test harness exercising the placeholderResendMessage feature against a controlled peer
  • Post-patch logs from a 6.7.22+ build where the field still appears but is now rejected by the library — confirm by checking for an accompanying rejection/drop log message
  • Self-chat / linked-device sync where the bot sees its own session protocolMessages legitimately
Suppression filter
| where SyslogMessage !has "dropped" and SyslogMessage !has "rejected"
Response runbook
1. TRIAGE — read 30 log lines either side of the hit. Confirm requestId came from an inbound message (not bot's own outbound). Check the JID/sender of the upsert against the bot's known peers; an unknown / never-seen JID is a strong positive. 2. CONTAIN — apply the article's workaround immediately: drop messages.upsert events containing requestId and disable shouldSyncHistoryMessage. Plan a fast-follow upgrade to 6.7.22 / 7.0.0-rc12 within 24h. 3. HUNT — for the same bot, look back 30 days for prior protocolMessage events from the same sender JID (this is the actor's exploitation window). Cross-check downstream actions: did the bot act on the spoofed messages (auto-replies, command execution, money transfer, etc.)?
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe" or FileName =~ "node.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("baileys", "@whiskeysockets/baileys")
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("baileys", "@whiskeysockets/baileys")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has "messages.upsert"
| where SyslogMessage has "requestId"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("protocolMessage", "placeholderResendMessage")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:(nodejs OR baileys OR application) "messages.upsert" "requestId" ("protocolMessage" OR "placeholderResendMessage")
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/node\.exe$/i CommandLine=/baileys/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, CommandLine], function=count())
APPLICATION
index=* (sourcetype=baileys OR sourcetype=nodejs OR source=*baileys*) "messages.upsert" "requestId" ("protocolMessage" OR "placeholderResendMessage")
| stats count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime by host source sourcetype
| sort - lastTime
Baileys app state sync integrity violation (corruption detection) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects high-volume mutations of Baileys auth/state files (creds.json, app-state-sync-key-*, app-state-sync-version-*, baileys_auth_info/ folder) within a short window — the on-disk symptom of the article's 'app state sync jamming' attack where injected fake key shares corrupt the local state store. Rationale: Article states the exploit 'corrupt[s] the app state sync system by sending fake key shares' — and the workaround section admits 'no workarounds for the app state sync jamming.' Baileys' useMultiFileAuthState ships state to canonical files (creds.json, app-state-sync-key-*, app-state-sync-version-*) — bursts of mutations on these are the disk symptom of the attack. Cross-checked: https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qvv5-jq5g-4cgg, Baileys source tree on https://github.com/WhiskeySockets/Baileys for the canonical state file names. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qvv5-jq5g-4cgg • https://github.com/WhiskeySockets/Baileys
ATT&CKT1565.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Initial pairing / first-time QR scan where the bot writes every state file fresh (expect single burst on day one of deployment)
  • Normal linked-device re-key after WhatsApp force-rotates session keys (rare but legitimate)
  • Application crash + restart loop that re-reads/re-writes state on every relaunch
  • Backup job snapshotting the state directory by copying files in place
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe" and FileChanges > 10 and not (Files has "creds.json" and array_length(Files) <= 2)
Response runbook
1. TRIAGE — count the burst: >10 file changes/5m is suspicious. Compare the involved keys against a known-good snapshot (md5 of creds.json, list of app-state-sync-key-* files) if FIM baseline exists. Look at the spawning process tree to confirm it's the Baileys-using Node service. 2. CONTAIN — stop the Node service to halt further state corruption. Restore the state directory from the last known-good backup; if no backup, plan a fresh QR re-pair (will invalidate any attacker-injected keys). 3. HUNT — correlate against UC3 (protocolMessage exploit signature) on the same host within ±10 minutes — that confirms exploit chain. Look for outbound WhatsApp traffic from the bot to unexpected JIDs after the corruption (data leak / spoof reach).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified", "FileRenamed", "FileDeleted")
| where (FolderPath contains @"\baileys_auth_info\" or FolderPath contains @"\auth_info_baileys\" or FolderPath contains @"\baileys-store\")
   or FileName startswith "app-state-sync-key-"
   or FileName startswith "app-state-sync-version-"
   or FileName =~ "creds.json"
| summarize FileChanges=count(), Files=make_set(FileName, 50), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, bin(Timestamp, 5m)
| where FileChanges > 10
| order by LastSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where (TargetFilePath contains @"\baileys_auth_info\" or TargetFilePath contains @"\auth_info_baileys\" or TargetFilePath contains @"\baileys-store\")
   or TargetFileName startswith "app-state-sync-key-"
   or TargetFileName startswith "app-state-sync-version-"
   or TargetFileName =~ "creds.json"
| summarize FileChanges=count(), Files=make_set(TargetFileName, 50), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where FileChanges > 10
| order by LastSeen desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:(*baileys_auth_info* OR *auth_info_baileys* OR *baileys-store* OR *app-state-sync-key-* OR *app-state-sync-version-* OR *\\creds.json)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/(baileys_auth_info|auth_info_baileys|baileys-store|app-state-sync-key-|app-state-sync-version-|creds\.json)/i

Baileys fake-message-key / signature-verification failures in app logs AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts for Signal-protocol verification errors logged by Baileys during message decryption — the symptom of the article's 'fake message key and payload' spoofing primitive. Bursts of these errors against a single peer JID strongly suggest active exploitation of CVE-2026-48063. Rationale: Article's core impact statement: the exploit 'allows anyone to spoof messages' via a 'fake message key and payload.' Signal-protocol verification phrases ('Bad MAC', 'signature verification failed', 'invalid message key') are the standard libsignal error messages Baileys logs to stderr when key/signature checks fail — the loud disk symptom of the spoofing primitive in flight. Defender/Falcon left empty: EDR doesn't ship Node app stderr. Cross-checked: https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qvv5-jq5g-4cgg, Baileys source for error-message strings. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qvv5-jq5g-4cgg • https://github.com/WhiskeySockets/Baileys
ATT&CKT1565.001
Data sourcesApplication logs (no CIM datamodel — raw Syslog/app)
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine WhatsApp protocol drift / WhatsApp-side key rotation causing legitimate one-off MAC failures (typically isolated, not bursty)
  • Bot restart mid-conversation losing session state and failing to decrypt in-flight messages
  • Out-of-order message delivery on poor mobile network where the local ratchet advances past a delayed message
  • Corrupted local state from disk error (pivot to UC4 to confirm)
  • Debug build with verbose protocol logging emitting these phrases on every successful decrypt-and-recover
Suppression filter
| where SyslogMessage !has "recovered" and SyslogMessage !has "retry"
Response runbook
1. TRIAGE — bucket the hits by sender JID and minute. A single sender repeatedly failing verification (>3 fails in 5m) is the high-fidelity exploit signal; scattered single fails across many senders is more likely network/protocol drift. 2. CONTAIN — for any suspect sender JID, block at the application layer (drop messages from that JID) and apply the article workaround: drop messages.upsert with requestId, disable history sync. Upgrade to 6.7.22 / 7.0.0-rc12. 3. HUNT — pivot to UC4 (same host, ±10 min) to confirm app state corruption; pivot to UC3 to confirm placeholderResendMessage chain. Pull the offending sender JID's full message history with the bot — anything the bot acted on while in spoofed state is suspect output.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("baileys", "@whiskeysockets/baileys")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("signature verification failed", "invalid message key", "key mismatch", "MAC verification failed", "decryption failed", "Bad MAC")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:(nodejs OR baileys OR application) ("signature verification failed" OR "invalid message key" OR "MAC verification failed" OR "decryption failed" OR "Bad MAC")
APPLICATION
index=* (sourcetype=baileys OR sourcetype=nodejs OR source=*baileys*) ("signature verification failed" OR "invalid message key" OR "key mismatch" OR "MAC verification failed" OR "decryption failed" OR "Bad MAC")
| stats count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime by host source sourcetype
| sort - lastTime
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Execution or file write of known GlassWorm / postmark-mcp sample SHA1 hashes · [LLM] npm / node postinstall hook spawning network-capable LOLBin (supply-chain post-install execution) · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Dev tooling beaconing to postmark-mcp / GlassWorm campaign infrastructure (giftshop.club, sfrclak.com) · [LLM] VS Code / Cursor / node reaching Solana blockchain RPC endpoints (GlassWorm C2 channel) · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Dev tooling beaconing to postmark-mcp / GlassWorm campaign infrastructure (giftshop.club, sfrclak.com) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts host-to-C2 callouts to the published Aikido IOC pack tied to the GlassWorm / postmark-mcp supply-chain compromise referenced in the article. Article-specific because it pivots on the exact IPs (142.11.206.73, 45.32.150.251, 45.32.151.157, 70.34.242.255) and domains (giftshop.club, sfrclak.com) the campaign uses for post-install exfil and second-stage download. Rationale: Direct match on the article's IOC pack: IPs 142.11.206.73, 45.32.150.251, 45.32.151.157, 70.34.242.255 and domains giftshop.club, sfrclak.com tied to the GlassWorm / postmark-mcp supply-chain compromise. Any single hit on a corporate dev endpoint is a strong post-compromise indicator. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/intel • https://threatfox.abuse.ch/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/002/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1195.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel researcher / red-team detonating GlassWorm sample in an isolated lab forwarding telemetry to prod SIEM
  • Security tooling (passive DNS scanner, attack-surface monitoring service) actively resolving the domains for enrichment
  • Stale DNS cache on a host previously compromised but already remediated, replaying the resolution on TTL refresh
  • Sinkholed IP — if a takedown party now owns the IP, the destination is benign but the alert still fires
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","SenseNdr.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe") or RemoteIP in (BadIPs)
Response runbook
1. TRIAGE: Pull DeviceProcessEvents around Timestamp on DeviceName to identify InitiatingProcessFileName + parent chain — confirm whether the call originated from npm/node, Code.exe, an MCP server binary, or a browser extension host. 2. CONTAIN: Isolate the device via MDE machine isolation; rotate any cloud / npm publish / SSH credentials present in the user profile (~/.npmrc, ~/.aws/, ~/.ssh/, ~/.gitconfig); revoke active session tokens for that user in Entra/Okta. 3. HUNT: Enumerate npm packages installed in the prior 24h (DeviceFileEvents on \node_modules\, package-lock.json writes) and any VS Code / Cursor extension installs (.vscode/extensions, .cursor/extensions) — fan out the same network query across the org to find peer infections.
let BadIPs = dynamic(["142.11.206.73","45.32.150.251","45.32.151.157","70.34.242.255"]);
let BadDomains = dynamic(["giftshop.club","sfrclak.com"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in (BadIPs) or RemoteUrl has_any (BadDomains)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
let BadIPs = dynamic(["142.11.206.73","45.32.150.251","45.32.151.157","70.34.242.255"]);
let BadDomains = dynamic(["giftshop.club","sfrclak.com"]);
union isfuzzy=true
  (ImDnsActivity
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where DnsQuery has_any (BadDomains)
   | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName, IndicatorType="DNS", Indicator=DnsQuery),
  (ImNetworkSession
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where DstIpAddr in (BadIPs) or DstHostname has_any (BadDomains)
   | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, DstPortNumber, IndicatorType="Network", Indicator=coalesce(DstHostname, DstIpAddr))
| order by TimeGenerated desc

VS Code / Cursor / node reaching Solana blockchain RPC endpoints (GlassWorm C2 channel) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts developer-tooling processes (Code.exe, Cursor.exe, node.exe, npm.exe) resolving or connecting to public Solana RPC infrastructure within a 5-minute window. The GlassWorm supply-chain attack referenced in the article uses Solana on-chain transactions as a resilient dead-drop C2 channel — a dev IDE talking to Solana RPC is rarely legitimate outside crypto-product teams. Rationale: GlassWorm (referenced by name in the article) is publicly documented to use Solana on-chain reads as a dead-drop C2 fetch — pinning the detection to dev IDEs and node runtime restricts the otherwise-noisy Solana DNS signal to the exact attack shape: a compromised VS Code/Cursor extension or npm postinstall script fetching its next-stage URL from a Solana transaction memo. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1102/ • https://blog.koi.security/ • https://www.aikido.dev/intel
ATT&CKT1102 T1568.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Engineers working on crypto / Web3 product lines whose dev workflows legitimately call Solana RPC
  • Developers running local @solana/web3.js test suites or hardhat/anchor toolchain
  • VS Code extensions for Solana development (e.g. Solana Developer Tools) doing legitimate RPC calls
  • node-based browser preview / linter background process bundling a wallet SDK fixture
Suppression filter
| where ActingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("@solana/web3.js","@coral-xyz/anchor","--web3-test","hardhat")
Response runbook
1. TRIAGE: Identify the parent of the dev-tool process — if it's electron/Code.exe spawned by a child extension host with --extension-id, capture the extension ID from CommandLine and check the marketplace for recent updates / takedowns. Inspect ~/.vscode/extensions and ~/.cursor/extensions for newly installed or recently updated packages. 2. CONTAIN: Isolate the device. Revoke npm publish tokens, GitHub PATs, and cloud creds in the user profile. Disable the suspect extension org-wide if a malicious extension ID is confirmed. 3. HUNT: Pivot on the extension ID across the fleet via DeviceFileEvents for the extension's manifest path; pivot on RemoteIP returned by the Solana DNS to find direct IP callouts that skipped DNS.
let SolanaDomains = dynamic(["solana.com","mainnet-beta.solana.com","api.mainnet-beta.solana.com","api.devnet.solana.com","api.testnet.solana.com","helius.xyz","helius-rpc.com","solscan.io","solana-rpc.com","genesysgo.net","quicknode.com"]);
let DevTools = dynamic(["Code.exe","Cursor.exe","node.exe","npm.exe","npx.exe","Code - Insiders.exe","WindsurfNext.exe","electron.exe"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (DevTools)
| where RemoteUrl has_any (SolanaDomains)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
let SolanaDomains = dynamic(["solana.com","mainnet-beta.solana.com","api.mainnet-beta.solana.com","api.devnet.solana.com","api.testnet.solana.com","helius.xyz","helius-rpc.com","solscan.io","solana-rpc.com","genesysgo.net","quicknode.com"]);
let DevTools = dynamic(["Code.exe","Cursor.exe","node.exe","npm.exe","npx.exe","Code - Insiders.exe","WindsurfNext.exe","electron.exe"]);
let WindowMin = 5m;
let DnsHits = ImDnsActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where DnsQuery has_any (SolanaDomains)
    | project DnsTime=TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DnsQuery;
ImProcessCreate

| where ActingProcessName has_any (DevTools)
| extend HostKey = coalesce(DvcHostname, "")
| join kind=inner (DnsHits | extend HostKey = coalesce(DvcHostname, SrcHostname, "")) on HostKey
| where TimeGenerated between (DnsTime - WindowMin .. DnsTime + WindowMin)
| project TimeGenerated, DnsTime, HostKey, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, DnsQuery
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Execution or file write of known GlassWorm / postmark-mcp sample SHA1 hashes AIInstallation High
Direct hash IOC match on the three SHA1s shipped with the article: 2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca, d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71, 07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766. Covers both execution (process create) and on-disk landing (file write) so we catch drops that haven't run yet. Rationale: The article ships three SHA1 hashes tied to the campaign discussed (GlassWorm / postmark-mcp). Direct hash hits on workstation telemetry are the highest-confidence signal we can ship — any positive is investigation-worthy regardless of process context. Cross-checked against: • https://threatfox.abuse.ch/ • https://bazaar.abuse.ch/ • https://www.aikido.dev/intel
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IR / malware analyst detonating one of these samples in a sandbox VM that ships telemetry to the production tenant
  • Threat-intel feed downloading samples to a designated analyst workstation for triage
  • Defender / Falcon sample-submission service caching the file in a quarantine path that still emits a FileWritten event
Response runbook
1. TRIAGE: Confirm the host is a real developer workstation (not a malware-analysis VM). Pull DeviceProcessEvents within ±5 min of the hash hit to identify what wrote it (npm install? a VS Code extension install? a Slack file download?) and what subsequently spawned. 2. CONTAIN: Immediately isolate via MDE/Falcon; rotate ALL credentials present in the user profile — npm publish tokens, GitHub PATs, AWS access keys, SSH keys, GPG signing keys, cloud SSO refresh tokens. Force re-auth across SSO. 3. HUNT: Pivot on the source package name (if npm postinstall — check ~/.npm/_logs and the parent npm command) and search the org for the same package install. Check git push activity from this workstation in the last 7 days for unreviewed pushes — assume any commits/publishes since first hash sighting are tainted.
let BadSHA1 = dynamic(["2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca","d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71","07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766"]);
union isfuzzy=true
  (DeviceProcessEvents
   | where Timestamp > ago(90d)
   | where SHA1 in (BadSHA1) or InitiatingProcessSHA1 in (BadSHA1)
   | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA1, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessSHA1, ProcessCommandLine, IndicatorType="ProcessExec"),
  (DeviceFileEvents
   | where Timestamp > ago(90d)
   | where SHA1 in (BadSHA1)
   | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA1, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, IndicatorType="FileWrite")
| order by Timestamp desc
let BadSHA1 = dynamic(["2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca","d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71","07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766"]);
union isfuzzy=true
  (ImProcessCreate
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
   | where SHA1 in (BadSHA1) or Hash in (BadSHA1)
   | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, SHA1, IndicatorType="ProcessExec"),
  (ImFileEvent
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
   | where TargetFileSHA1 in (BadSHA1) or Hash in (BadSHA1)
   | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA1, IndicatorType="FileWrite")
| order by TimeGenerated desc
